releases.headline: The minimum runtime moves to Node 24.22.1, which fixes the Brotli decoder flaw CVE-2026-111497
releases.summary: This release requires Node 24.22.1 or newer. A host running any release from 24.19.0 through 24.22.0 needs its runtime upgraded before installing or starting this version. The published container image runs Node 26.12.1 against libbrotli 1.2.1, both of which carry the fix for CVE-2026-111497, so an operator running the image has nothing to change.

items.title: An alias can be stopped without being removed
items.body: The alias list in the operator interface carries a Stop control on every delivering alias and a Start control on every stopped one. Stopping an alias refuses mail to it at the wire and keeps the row, its destination and its history; mail to a stopped alias does not fall through to the domain's catch-all. Both directions ask for a reason and record it in the audit trail under `alias.status_changed`. Removing an alias still deletes the row, so an address you mean to silence for a while is stopped rather than removed.

items.title: The browser interface lists the files a message carries and serves them
items.body: A conversation now lists every file on each message it shows, with the name the sender gave it, the media type the sender declared and the size of the decoded bytes, and each row links to the file. The link is `/mail/<folder>/<message>/parts/<number>`, where the number is the body part number of RFC 9051 section 6.4.5, so a file is `2` on a message whose first part is its text and `1.2` inside a nested part. A file is served with `Content-Type: application/octet-stream` and `Content-Disposition: attachment` whatever the sender declared it to be, so a part claiming `text/html` is downloaded rather than rendered as a page on the server's own origin, and the response carries `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and `Cache-Control: private, no-store`. The disposition names the file in both forms RFC 6266 asks for: an ASCII `filename` and the `filename*` form of RFC 8187 carrying a name that has no ASCII spelling. The name shown on the page and the name the download is saved under are produced separately, so a name carrying a right-to-left override reads with its real extension on the page and is written to disk with the override replaced. The route resolves the folder against the signed-in account and the message inside it, and answers 404 for a folder or a message another account holds, for a part number nothing holds, and for the message's own text body, all with the same page. A message larger than 8 MiB is not opened, so its files are not listed and not served, and the conversation says so.

items.title: A reference for every module and primitive is served at /wiki
items.body: `/wiki` serves an index of every module and primitive in the running build, a page for each module and each primitive with its signature, status, options, examples and source location, and a specification index at `/wiki/specs` listing each cited RFC and standard with the primitives citing it. The server generates the pages from the documentation comments in `lib/` when the web interface starts. A signed-in account can read every page. A visitor with no session can read them while the public site is published through `BLAMEPOST_PUBLIC_SITE_ENABLED` or the console switch, and is sent to the sign-in page otherwise. A page served without a session carries `Cache-Control: private, max-age=900`, the header the front page carries, so a proxy or a CDN does not store a page holding one reader's CSRF token. The front page links `/wiki` in its navigation and the sitemap lists it. If a documentation comment cannot be turned into a page, the rest of the web interface still starts: webmail, the administration console and `/jmap` answer as usual, every GET at or below `/wiki` answers 503, and the front page and the sitemap stop listing `/wiki`. The server writes the reason to its error log and to the audit trail under `blamepost.web.wiki_unavailable`, with the source file and line of the comment.

items.title: Each mail listener's line ceiling is a setting, and the shipped numbers are published
items.body: Every listener bounds how many octets of one command line it will hold while it waits for a terminator, and that bound is now `listeners.<name>.maxLineBytes`. The shipped values are 1024 octets for the MX, submission and POP3 listeners and 8192 for IMAP and ManageSieve, which are the numbers those listeners already applied, so nothing about what this server accepts changes. What changes is that the numbers are stated: they are listed in the operator guide beside the other ceilings, and an installation that needs a different one sets it per listener as a whole number between 512 and 65536. A value outside that range is refused at start rather than at the socket. The floor is the 512 octets RFC 5321 section 4.5.3.1.4 requires an SMTP server to accept. This bounds a line that never ends; a command that does end meets its own protocol's grammar first, so a POP3 command over the 255 octets of RFC 2449 section 4 is still refused naming that number.

items.title: `blobs repair` ends a mailbox being charged for mail no protocol can list
items.body:
`blobs report` names a mailbox whose quota counter disagrees with the messages in it, and had nothing to offer about it. Filing a message writes the sealed octets, then the message store's row, then the row binding that message to a mailbox, and the counter moves on the second. A process that stops before the third leaves the counter charged for a message the owner can neither read nor delete, and the mailbox fills up against nothing.

Stop the server and run `blamepost blobs repair --confirm --reason <text>`. It destroys the messages the message store holds that no mailbox row names, and the counter falls by exactly what went. It writes no counter of its own: the message store's arithmetic moves the number, so a mailbox that reads as reconciled afterwards is one that is. `blobs report` now says per mailbox how many messages the repair would take and how many bytes they hold, so the decision is made on a number before anything is destroyed. The bodies those messages named are referenced by nothing afterwards, and `blobs reclaim` frees them once they have settled.

A preservation order and the retention floor keep a message here exactly as they keep any other. One they kept is named with the rule keeping it, and its mailbox stays charged for it. Where the message store counts FEWER messages than the mailbox lists, nothing here raises the counter: the run names those mailboxes, says that removing mail cannot close them, and exits non-zero rather than reporting the volume repaired. The run records `blamepost.store.blobs.quota_repaired`, naming who ran it, the reason they gave, and how much went and stayed.

items.title: A message records whether it carries files, and every surface answers from that one mark
items.body:
Every message this server files records whether it carries parts a client should offer as downloadable, as the IMAP keyword `$HasAttachment` or `$HasNoAttachment`. An IMAP client sees the keyword in `FETCH FLAGS`; a JMAP client reads `hasAttachment` on `Email/get`, which RFC 8621 section 4.1.4 defines from the same question; and the folder listing and the search results carry a Files mark on the rows that have one.

The answer is read off the message when it is filed rather than derived when it is read, so an `Email/get` naming several hundred identifiers costs no stored-body reads. It is a boolean and not a count: a number would need a keyword namespace of its own, which then appears in the tag list of every client that lists keywords, so the listing says a message carries files and does not say how many.

There are three answers rather than two. A message above the 8 MiB octet read bound is not opened, so it records neither keyword, the listing says the answer is not known for it, and `hasAttachment` answers true rather than reporting a message that is large precisely because it is carrying something as bare.

The two keywords are the server's. A JMAP `Email/set` naming one is refused with a `SetError`, a whole-keyword-set replacement leaves it where it is, and an IMAP `STORE` that adds or removes one is answered `NO`. An IMAP `APPEND` may carry either, which is what a client copying a mailbox across from another server sends, and the answer this server reads off the octets is written in its place.

items.title: `blamepost attachments` records that mark for the mail already on the volume
items.body:
Mail filed before this release records neither keyword. `blamepost attachments report` says how many stored messages record the answer and how many record nothing. `blamepost attachments backfill` opens the octets of the ones that record nothing and writes it. Both hold the data volume, so stop the server before running either.

Each message is marked on its own, so a run that stops partway has done everything it reached and running it again reaches the rest. `--limit <n>` caps how many messages one run opens, and the answer says how many it left. A message above the 8 MiB read bound, and one whose stored body cannot be read back, stay unmarked and are counted apart from the messages the run finished; the second is named one per line and sends you to `blamepost blobs report --verify`. A run files one audit row under `blamepost.mail.mailbox.attachment_marks_recorded` carrying its counts, and exits non-zero when a stored body could not be read.

Until it has run, a JMAP client is told those messages may carry files and the folder listing says the answer is not known for them, so nothing is hidden by the mark being absent.

items.title: IMAP `CREATE` makes a mailbox, so a mail client's new folder control works
items.body:
`CREATE` was answered `NO CREATE not configured`, so the only mailboxes an account ever had were the six it was provisioned with and every client's new folder control failed. RFC 9051 section 6.3.4 makes the command part of IMAP4rev2, which this server advertises. It now creates the mailbox, and `LIST`, `SELECT`, `STATUS` and `APPEND` all answer for what it made.

The hierarchy separator is `/`. A name ending in one is the declaration RFC 9051 section 6.3.4 describes and is not part of the name created, so `CREATE Projects/` makes `Projects`. A separator inside the name creates the superior levels the new one needs, so `CREATE Clients/Acme/2026` makes all three and each is a mailbox that opens.

A name is refused with the response code that says what to do about it: `[ALREADYEXISTS]` for a name that is already there, which includes every case of `INBOX`, `[CANNOT]` for a name this server will not keep, and `[LIMIT]` for an account that already holds the 1000 mailboxes one account may have. A name is compared as written, so `Statements` and `statements` are two mailboxes; `INBOX` is the one name matched without regard to case, which RFC 9051 section 5.1 requires.

The name is screened before it is stored, by the rule every mailbox name on this server passes, so a name carrying a control character, a bidirectional override, an invisible formatting character, a `LIST` wildcard, an empty level or a level spelled like a message address is refused rather than kept. The screen runs per level, because a level is a name a client addresses on its own.

That rule gained one entry with this release: a level spelled `.` or `..` is refused. A mailbox name is written into a URL path segment by the browser surface, and in a path `a/../b` names `b`, so such a level is a name that addresses somewhere other than where it reads. No mailbox could carry one before this release, because nothing created a mailbox, so no stored name is affected.

`DELETE`, `RENAME`, `SUBSCRIBE` and `UNSUBSCRIBE` answer as well; the entry below covers them.

items.title: `SELECT` and `EXAMINE` say which flags the mailbox keeps
items.body:
Neither command sent the `PERMANENTFLAGS` response, which RFC 9051 section 6.3.2 requires. A client that is not sent one is entitled to assume every flag it sends is kept permanently, so it offers the account holder marks the mailbox will not hold, and offers no way to invent a keyword of their own even where the mailbox would have kept it.

A read-write selection now names the five system flags this server keeps, `\Seen`, `\Answered`, `\Flagged`, `\Deleted` and `\Draft`, and `\*`, which says a client may create keywords of its own. It may: a keyword an account holder's client invents is written through to the message store and read back by that account's other sessions.

A selection opened with `EXAMINE` names no flags at all. Section 6.3.2 permits no change to the permanent state of a mailbox opened read-only, and a `STORE` from such a session is refused, so an empty list is what that session can keep.

`$HasAttachment` and `$HasNoAttachment` appear in the `FLAGS` list and not in `PERMANENTFLAGS`. A message in the mailbox carries one of them and a client may not set either, which is the distinction the two responses draw.

items.title: A JMAP client can fetch the files a message carries
items.body:
The session document has always named a `downloadUrl`, and `Email/get` reports `hasAttachment` off the mark written when a message is filed, so a client was told a message carried a file and was handed a route that answered `503 serverUnavailable` on every fetch. That route now serves the octets.

A client fills in the template the session document names, `/jmap/download/{accountId}/{blobId}/{name}?accept={type}`, which is the URI template of RFC 8620 section 6.2. The accountId has to be the one the signed-in account is enumerated for, and the blobId names what is served. A blob id is either a message identifier, which answers that message's raw octets and is the value `Email.blobId` carries, or that identifier followed by `-p` and the body part number of RFC 9051 section 6.4.5 with each dot written as a dash, because RFC 8620 section 1.2 admits no dot in an id. The file that is `2` on a message whose first part is its text therefore downloads under `<message>-p2`, and one at `1.2` inside a nested part under `<message>-p1-2`.

Every blob is served with `Content-Type: application/octet-stream` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` whatever the sender declared and whatever the `accept` variable asked for, so a part claiming `text/html` is downloaded rather than rendered as a page on the server's own origin. `Content-Disposition: attachment` names the file in both forms RFC 6266 section 4.1 asks for, an ASCII `filename` and the `filename*` form of RFC 8187, and the name comes from the message rather than from the `name` variable in the URL, so the caller does not choose what a receiver writes to disk.

The blob is resolved under the signed-in account, and the parts it reaches are the parts the browser interface lists for the same message. A blob id another account holds, an identifier nothing holds, a part number nothing holds, a part that is the message's own text, a message larger than 8 MiB and an id outside the RFC 8620 section 1.2 grammar all answer the same 404 problem document, so one refusal cannot be told from another.

Blob upload is unchanged: `/jmap/upload/{accountId}` still answers 503 and the session document advertises `maxSizeUpload` as 1 octet, the smallest value the framework accepts, and ROADMAP.md tracks it. A client takes these blob ids out of `Email/get` rather than building them from the grammar above; the entry below covers that.

items.title: An IMAP client can remove, rename and subscribe to a mailbox
items.body:
`DELETE`, `RENAME`, `SUBSCRIBE` and `UNSUBSCRIBE` were answered `NO <verb> not configured`, so a client could make a folder and never remove or rename it, and its subscribed-folder view had nothing to read. RFC 9051 sections 6.3.5 to 6.3.8 make all four part of IMAP4rev2, which this server advertises. All four now answer, and `LIST` reads the arguments and options RFC 9051 section 6.3.9 gives it.

`DELETE` removes the mailbox and destroys the mail it holds, through the same delete path as `EXPUNGE`. A legal hold and the retention floor decide each message there, so a mailbox holding a message they keep is not removed: the command is answered `NO [CONTACTADMIN]` naming how many messages were kept and how many were destroyed, and the mailbox is still there holding what stayed. Sending the command again destroys nothing further and answers the same way, so a client retrying it cannot walk past the hold. Set `BLAMEPOST_COMPLIANCE_POSTURE` to see the retention floor take part.

A session that deletes the mailbox it has selected, or renames `INBOX` while holding it, is answered `* OK [CLOSED]` ahead of the tagged `OK` and returns to the authenticated state. Another session of the same account holding that mailbox is sent an untagged `BYE` and disconnected, because IMAP has no response that closes another session's selection; its client reconnects and selects again.

`DELETE INBOX` is refused, which section 6.3.5 calls an error, and so are `Sent`, `Drafts`, `Trash`, `Junk` and `Archive`: this server files a sent copy and a moved message into those by name, so an account without one has a delivery path with nowhere to land. Removing a mailbox that has names underneath it removes only the name it was given, which section 6.3.5 requires. The level stays in a listing under the `\NonExistent` attribute of section 7.3.1, alongside `\HasChildren`, so a client can still reach what is under it, and `SELECT` of that name is answered `NO [NONEXISTENT]`.

`RENAME` moves the names underneath the mailbox with it and creates the superior levels the new name needs. The mailbox keeps its `UIDVALIDITY` and every message keeps its UID, so a client's cache survives the rename. Renaming `INBOX` moves the messages into a new mailbox and leaves `INBOX` in place, empty, with its own inferior names untouched, which section 6.3.6 writes out; the new mailbox takes a `UIDVALIDITY` of its own. A rename onto a name that exists is answered `NO [ALREADYEXISTS]`, one from a name that does not is `NO [NONEXISTENT]`, and a rename of a mailbox into its own hierarchy is refused.

`SUBSCRIBE` records a name for the account and `UNSUBSCRIBE` removes it. The record outlives the mailbox, which section 6.3.8 requires: removing a subscribed mailbox leaves the name in the account's subscribed set, listed as a name that does not exist, until the client unsubscribes from it. `SUBSCRIBE` of a name the account does not hold is answered `NO [NONEXISTENT]`.

`LIST` matched neither its reference nor its pattern, so every narrowed question was answered with the whole namespace. It now matches both, with `%` stopping at the hierarchy separator and `*` crossing it, takes a parenthesized list of patterns, and serves the `SUBSCRIBED` and `REMOTE` selection options and the `SUBSCRIBED`, `CHILDREN` and `STATUS` return options. `LIST (SUBSCRIBED) "" "*"` lists the subscribed set alone and `LIST "" "*" RETURN (SUBSCRIBED)` marks it; `RETURN (STATUS (MESSAGES UNSEEN))` carries the counts beside each name. `RECURSIVEMATCH` is answered `BAD` naming the option, and so is a reference and pattern coming to more than 256 bytes or carrying more than 16 wildcards, which is the bound on how much matching one command can ask for.

One residue to know about: the message store this server composes creates folders and does not remove them, so a removed mailbox leaves an empty folder row there, holding no mail and reachable by no name. ROADMAP.md tracks it.

items.title: A JMAP client reads the files on a message out of `Email/get`
items.body:
`hasAttachment` told a client a message carried a file and the session document handed it a download route, and nothing told it the blob ids that route resolves, so it could only build one by reading the id grammar. `Email/get` now answers the `attachments` list of RFC 8621 section 4.1.4, and a client takes each `blobId` out of the message and fills it straight into `downloadUrl`.

A call whose `properties` argument carries `attachments` is answered the list; a call that leaves `properties` out, or names other properties, carries no `attachments` at all. Section 4.2 has the property in its default set, and this server answers it only to a call that names it: building the list opens each message and walks its structure, and one call may name 500 identifiers against the 8 MiB read bound. Measured over 50 messages each carrying a 256 KiB file, naming the property adds about 300 ms and reads 12.5 MiB; over 50 messages that carry no file it adds nothing measurable, because the mark written when each was filed already records that there is nothing to list.

Each part carries `partId`, `blobId`, `size`, `name`, `type`, `charset`, `disposition`, `cid`, `language` and `location`. `partId` is the body part number of RFC 9051 section 6.4.5, which is the number the browser interface addresses the same part by, and `size` is the octet count after transfer decoding, which is the `Content-Length` the download answers with. `name` and `type` are both screened before they are sent, so a value carrying a reading-order override arrives reading the way its bytes do, and a part the sender did not name answers null rather than a name this server chose. `headers` and `subParts` are not answered: every part in the list is a leaf. `bodyProperties` is not read, so a client naming it is answered the whole set above.

A message with no file answers an empty list beside `hasAttachment: false`. A message larger than 8 MiB is not opened, so it answers `hasAttachment: true` and carries no `attachments` property at all: an empty list there would report no files on the one message whose files this server declined to look at, and a client that asked for the property can see that it is missing.

A `properties` argument that is not a list of names is refused with `invalidArguments` on every `/get` this server answers, rather than read past.

The parts this lists are the parts the browser interface lists for the same message and the parts a blob id reaches, which is one reading of what a file is rather than three.

items.title: Node 24.22.1 is the minimum runtime
items.body: `engines.node` is `>=24.22.1`. `.nvmrc`, every workflow Node pin, the README requirements and the CONTRIBUTING requirements state the same version. Upgrade Node before running `npm install` or before starting `bin/blamepost.js` on a host. 24.22.1 is the current release of the Node 24 line, which receives security patches until April 2028.

items.title: The vendored framework is blamejs 0.21.8
items.body: `lib/vendor/blamejs/` moves from 0.18.61 to 0.21.8. The releases in between carry the upstream fixes to DKIM signing over repeated headers, DANE trust-anchor validation, X.509 path-length and name constraints, OCSP response binding, SMTP end-of-data smuggling detection, IMAP quoted mailbox names and POP3 dot-stuffing, among others; the blamejs changelog lists each. 0.21.6 refuses on any Node release the inputs that reach the October 2026 Node.js flaws: a TLS dial to an IPv4 address in a non-canonical spelling such as `127.1`, a pooled HTTPS connection read for a response the server wrote unprompted (CVE-2026-105481), and a recipient domain that is not a DNS name, which a NUL byte could truncate (CVE-2026-105482). It also refuses at boot a runtime without the Brotli fix or with an OpenSSL older than 3.4.8, 3.5.9, 3.6.5 or 4.0.3 on its release line (CVE-2026-35189). The published image runs Node 26.12.1 with OpenSSL 4.0.3, and Node 24.22.1 bundles OpenSSL 3.5.9, so both pass. A host install whose Node uses an older system OpenSSL does not start until that library is upgraded. 0.21.7 turns TLS certificate compression off on every listener and every outbound connection, because OpenSSL decompresses a peer's certificate before the chain is verified. 0.21.8 retries a DNS lookup answered SERVFAIL or REFUSED as a temporary failure rather than reading it as a permanent one.The JMAP listener now requires the limits a session document advertises to be the ones it enforces, which moves the advertised JMAP limits to the framework's strict profile, described under the JMAP entry below. There is nothing to configure.

items.title: IMAP no longer advertises QRESYNC, NOTIFY or CATENATE
items.body: The capability line in the IMAP greeting, in the answer to `CAPABILITY` and in the `AUTHENTICATE` completion no longer names `QRESYNC`, `NOTIFY` or `CATENATE`, and none of the three was served. After `ENABLE QRESYNC` an expunge was still reported with `EXPUNGE` rather than `VANISHED`, and a `SELECT` carrying a `QRESYNC` parameter never reported the messages expunged since the client's last visit, so a client synchronizing with QRESYNC kept expunged messages in its cache. `NOTIFY` and `CATENATE` were answered `NO`. `ENABLE QRESYNC` now completes with an `ENABLED` response that does not list it, `ENABLE` before authentication is answered `BAD`, and a `SELECT` or `EXAMINE` carrying a `QRESYNC` parameter is answered `BAD`. `CONDSTORE`, `METADATA` and `METADATA-SERVER` are still advertised and served. A client reads the capability line when it connects, so a client that used QRESYNC synchronizes with CONDSTORE from its next connection.

items.title: Retiring a signing pair and removing one leg of an alias ask for a value that names one row
items.body: Retiring a signing pair in the admin console asked for its selector, and the default selector `bp<YYYYMM>` is the same on every domain keyed in the same month, so the selector confirmed a press on any of those domains. It now asks for the name the pair's record is published at, `<selector>._domainkey.<domain>`, and a domain and selector naming no active pair are refused before anything is asked. Removing an alias asked for its address, or the domain for a catch-all, and every leg of a fan-out shares that value. While another row shares it, the console now asks for the destination of the leg being removed.

items.title: The container release reports the image digest instead of a hash of a local archive
items.body: The run that builds and pushes `ghcr.io/blamejs/blamepost` reported a SHA3-512 taken over a `docker save` stream of the image it had just pulled. That value is not reproducible: the push is a multi-architecture index, `docker pull` materializes only the runner's own architecture out of it, and the archive layout depends on the engine version writing it, so an operator on arm64 computing the same hash gets a different answer. It is replaced by the image digest, which is the `sha256:` value the registry serves, the same on every architecture, and the reference SECURITY.md's verification recipes take: `cosign verify ghcr.io/blamejs/blamepost@sha256:<digest>`, and the value a deployment pins instead of a moving tag.

items.title: The browser names the folder in the query string rather than in the path
items.body:
A mailbox page was `/mail/<folder>` and a message page was `/mail/<folder>/<message>`. The folder now travels in the query: `/mail?folder=<folder>` for the mailbox, `/mail/<message>?folder=<folder>` for a message, and `/mail/<message>/parts/<part>?folder=<folder>` for a file on it. A folder name carries the hierarchy delimiter and may carry a backslash, and a path segment holds neither.

A bookmark saved against the old shape is answered `404 No such folder`, because the segment it carries is now read as a message identifier. Open the folder from the folder list and save the link again. A link that names no folder still opens the inbox.

items.title: Archiving or suspending the last administrator by address is refused before the console asks for the address
items.body: The account actions in the admin console accept an address in the `id` field as well as an account id. With an address there, the check for whether the action would leave an administrator able to sign in counted the account being acted on, so the console asked the operator to type the address and a reason for a change it then refused. The check now counts against the account the field resolves to, and the refusal comes on the first post.

items.title: An IMAP SELECT or EXAMINE that fails leaves no mailbox selected
items.body: After a refused `SELECT` or `EXAMINE`, the mailbox selected before it stayed selected, so an `EXPUNGE` sent next removed the messages flagged `\Deleted` in a mailbox the client no longer had open. A `SELECT` or `EXAMINE` that fails, whether it is answered `NO` or `BAD`, now leaves the session with no mailbox selected, as RFC 9051 section 6.3.2 requires, and a command that needs a selected mailbox is refused. A mailbox the account does not hold is answered `NO [NONEXISTENT]`.

items.title: A mailbox opened with EXAMINE is not changed by the session that opened it
items.body: `EXPUNGE` from a session that opened the mailbox with `EXAMINE` removed the messages flagged `\Deleted`, and a `FETCH` of `BODY[]`, `RFC822` or `RFC822.TEXT` from one set `\Seen`. RFC 9051 section 6.3.3 opens such a mailbox read-only. `EXPUNGE` from a read-only session is now answered `NO` and removes nothing, and a read from one leaves the message's flags unchanged. Each session keeps its own mode, so a read-only session stays read-only while another session of the same account has the same mailbox open with `SELECT`.

items.title: IMAP CLOSE removes the messages flagged \Deleted
items.body: `CLOSE` returned the session to the authenticated state and removed nothing. It now removes every message flagged `\Deleted` from a mailbox opened with `SELECT`, through the same delete path `EXPUNGE` takes, so a message under legal hold or inside the retention floor stays. It sends no untagged `EXPUNGE`, as RFC 9051 section 6.4.1 requires, and removes nothing from a mailbox opened with `EXAMINE`. `CLOSE` with no mailbox selected is answered `BAD`.

items.title: IMAP SELECT and EXAMINE accept the CONDSTORE parameter
items.body: `SELECT INBOX (CONDSTORE)` was read as a request for a mailbox named `INBOX (CONDSTORE)` and refused, so a client that opens mailboxes this way could open none. The parameter RFC 7162 section 3.1.8 defines is now read, the mailbox opens, and every `FETCH` response in the session afterwards carries `MODSEQ`. Any other select parameter is answered `BAD`.

items.title: An IMAP FETCH or STORE naming one message reads that message and no other
items.body: `FETCH` and `STORE` read the flags of every message in the mailbox before narrowing to the messages the command named. Each of those reads opens the message's sealed fields, and together they block every other connection the server holds. On a mailbox of 1,000 messages, `FETCH 1 (UID)` took 4.9 seconds and `STORE 1 +FLAGS (\Seen)` took 5.1 seconds. Both commands now read only the messages their sequence set names, and `FETCH` reads flags only when an attribute needs them, which is `FLAGS` or a read that sets `\Seen`. `FETCH 1:* (FLAGS)`, `STATUS` with `UNSEEN`, `SEARCH` and `EXPUNGE` still read every message in the mailbox.

items.title: An IMAP IDLE ended by a disconnect leaves nothing scheduled
items.body: When a client disconnected during `IDLE`, the 29-minute limit on the `IDLE` stayed scheduled and kept the session's socket and state in memory until it fired. The limit is now canceled when the connection closes.

items.title: An IMAP STORE command takes one mod-sequence per 500 messages
items.body: `STORE` gave every message it changed a mod-sequence of its own, so `STORE 1:500 +FLAGS (\Seen)` advanced the mailbox's mod-sequence by 500. The message store sets that counter from the clock when it expunges a message, so a counter that had advanced faster than the clock was set back, and the next `STORE` could be given a mod-sequence lower than one already reported, which RFC 7162 section 3.1 forbids. A CONDSTORE client asking for changes since the higher value then missed that change. `STORE` now takes one mod-sequence for `+FLAGS` and `-FLAGS`, and one per distinct set of flags removed for `FLAGS`, for each 500 messages it changes, which RFC 7162 permits. The browser and JMAP read a mailbox in pages ordered by mod-sequence, and the 500 bound keeps every message sharing one inside a single read, so a `STORE` over a large mailbox leaves every message reachable. The counter can still be set back by a clock stepped backwards on the host.

items.title: A reply written in the browser threads and titles itself correctly
items.body: Replies and forwards opened from a message now take their recipients, subject and threading headers from the outbound composer rather than deriving them again in the browser interface. Five results change. A subject already carrying a reply prefix in any of the spellings clients write, including `Aw:`, `Sv:`, `Antw:`, `Odp:`, `Res:` and `Re[2]:`, gains one `Re:` instead of stacking a second prefix, and the same holds for `Fw:`, `WG:`, `TR:` and `Doorst:` on a forward. A `References` chain names each ancestor once and is cut to twenty ids, keeping the root of the conversation and the most recent ancestors, so a long thread stays inside the header size a receiver will take. A forward no longer sets `In-Reply-To`, which said the forwarded message was being answered. Reply-all leaves off every address the replying account holds rather than only the one the reply is written under, so answering a message addressed to a departmental alias no longer copies the alias back to the mailbox behind it. And a forward carries the sender, date and subject of the message it forwards above the quoted body.

items.title: Quoting a message that has only an HTML body shows what was read
items.body: A reply to a message with an HTML body and no plain-text alternative used to carry fragments of the markup into the draft: script source, attribute values and undecoded character references all reached the body the account holder sent onward. The quote is now the text the message displayed, with character references resolved, and it is cut at 64 KiB so answering a very long message does not put the whole of it back on the wire.

items.title: JMAP reports the References header a message carried
items.body: `Email/get` and `EmailSubmission/set` read the stored `References` list directly. A message with no `Message-ID` of its own was previously reported with its chain one id short.

items.title: A JMAP request the server refuses is answered with its RFC 8620 problem type
items.body: `POST /jmap/api` accepted a request sent as `text/plain`, and answered a malformed request with `invalidArguments` or `limit/maxCallsInRequest` in a body that carried no `status`. The route now answers `400` with an `application/problem+json` document: `urn:ietf:params:jmap:error:notJSON` for a `Content-Type` other than `application/json` or an empty body, `notRequest` for JSON that is not a request object, `limit` with a `limit` member naming `maxCallsInRequest`, `maxBackRefDepth` or `maxConcurrentRequests`, and `unknownCapability`. A method call with no `accountId`, or with an `ids` or `destroy` list holding something other than ids, is refused `invalidArguments`, where it answered `serverFail`. A body the request parser cannot read as JSON, and a body over 10 MiB, are still refused by that parser with `400` and `413` before JMAP reads them.

items.title: A JMAP submission sends to the draft's Cc and Bcc recipients
items.body: `EmailSubmission/set` with no `envelope` sent the draft to its `To` addresses only and left the `Cc` field off the message. It now sends to the `To`, `Cc` and `Bcc` addresses, writes the `Cc` field, and keeps `Bcc` off the message that leaves. An `update` or `destroy` naming a submission id is reported `notFound`, where the answer named neither.

items.title: `restore apply` works on the data volume the published image mounts
items.body: In the published image the data directory is the mount point of a volume and the image's user cannot write beside it, so `restore apply` stopped with `EACCES` creating `/var/lib/blamepost.rollbacks` and left a decrypted copy of the bundle under `/tmp`. A restore now decrypts the bundle into `.restore/incoming-<moment>/` on the data volume, moves every entry at the top of the volume except `blamepost.lock` and `.restore` into `.restore/<moment>/`, and moves the bundle's entries into their place. The data directory itself is not renamed, and its owner and mode stay as they were. `restore rollback` and `restore list-rollbacks` read rollback points from `.restore`. Rollback points an earlier version kept beside the volume in `<data directory>.rollbacks` are no longer listed, and can be deleted once they are not needed.

items.title: A bundle no longer carries the volume lock
items.body: `backup run` put `blamepost.lock` into every bundle, naming the process that took the bundle. A restore in another container found a lock recorded in another process namespace, refused to open the restored volume and put the previous one back. Bundles now leave out `blamepost.lock` and `.restore`, and a restore does not write either name from a bundle an earlier version wrote.

items.title: An interrupted restore is refused at the next open and undone by `restore rollback`
items.body: `restore apply` and `restore rollback` write `.restore/in-flight.json` before each half of the move and remove it once the volume is settled. While the file exists, every command that opens the volume, `serve` included, refuses with `store/restore-interrupted`. `blamepost restore rollback --confirm --reason <text>` puts back the volume that was there before the interrupted command started. A process killed partway through a restore previously left the data directory missing, and the next command created an empty volume in its place.

items.title: `restore rollback` takes only this volume's rollback points, and puts the live volume back when a point does not open
items.body: `--point` accepted any existing path, moved the live volume aside and put that path in its place. It now takes a path `restore list-rollbacks` prints, or a point's name, and refuses anything else with exit `2`. A rollback point that does not open is moved back into the point, the entries that were live are put back, and the command exits `1`.

items.title: Backup retention counts only bundles that verify
items.body: `backup run --keep` deleted older bundles before the new one had been read back, and both it and `backup purge` counted every directory in storage whose name looked like a bundle id. A bundle cut short, one written under another passphrase, or a directory carrying a later id with nothing in it was kept in place of a bundle that restores. Both now keep the newest `--keep` bundles whose manifest reads, whose signature is from an audit signing key the volume holds or held, whose files are all present at the listed sizes, and which the passphrase file opens, and they delete only older bundles that pass the same check. Anything else is neither counted nor deleted, and the command lists it with the reason. `backup run` deletes nothing when its own bundle does not verify, and `backup purge` exits `1` and deletes nothing when storage holds bundles and none of them verifies.

items.title: The reporting verbs refuse a volume whose schema is not the one this release reads
items.body: While the server holds the volume, `account list`, `account show`, `domain list`, `domain show`, `dkim list`, `dkim records`, `zone preview`, `zone verify`, `zone verify-token`, `credential list`, `credential show`, `credential bounces`, `reports list`, `reports show`, `blobs report`, `audit verify-chain` and `doctor` read it through a read-only open, and that open does not update the schema. Against a volume last opened for writing by an older release, `reports list` failed with a SQLite error such as `no such column: verifiedOrgDomain`, and the other verbs answered from a schema this release does not read. Each of these verbs now refuses with `store/snapshot-schema-behind` and names up to eight of the tables, columns and migrations the volume lacks. Start the server on the new release, or stop the server and run the verb again, which opens the volume for writing and updates the schema; the verbs then answer while the server runs. A volume that records a migration this release does not ship is refused with `store/snapshot-schema-ahead`. The refused open removes its decrypted working copy, and nothing on the volume is written.

items.title: `queue show` reports the size of the message that is waiting
items.body: The size line printed `undefined byte(s)`, because the verb never carried a size. It now measures the body on the volume and prints its byte count. A descriptor whose body is gone says so in that line instead of printing a value, which is the state `queue list` already reports as an unreadable entry: a number cannot tell a missing body apart from one of no bytes, and the two want different work.

items.title: A data directory that cannot be one names the setting rather than raising a path
items.body: `BLAMEPOST_DATA_DIR` naming a regular file was accepted at start and failed later as `EEXIST: file already exists, mkdir '<path>'`, which names neither the variable nor the entry underneath it. It is now refused while the configuration is read, with the variable and the resolved path in the message, so `blamepost doctor` reports it without creating anything. The entries derived from it answer the same way: a file sitting where `blobs/`, `queue/`, `keys/` or `tls/` goes, and a directory sitting where `db.enc` goes, are each named and refused before any of them is created. A creation the filesystem refuses for another reason, such as a read-only mount or a directory this server may not write in, now carries the entry that asked for it alongside the system's own message.

items.title: A DKIM canonicalization or header set the signer cannot use is refused at start
items.body: The signer for a domain is built the first time that domain signs, so a `canonicalization` outside the four forms RFC 6376 section 3.4 defines, or a `headersToSign` entry that is not a header name, started cleanly and then sent every message from every hosted domain unsigned. Both are read when the DKIM handle is built, and the refusal names the accepted forms.

items.title: A delivery report the outbound path refuses is recorded rather than counted as sent
items.body: A delivery report is a message and goes out over the same outbound path as any other, so that path can refuse it the moment it is handed over: the sender's own domain publishes no mail exchanger, or publishes the RFC 7505 null MX, or `BLAMEPOST_OUTBOUND_RETRY` allows one attempt, which makes the report's first attempt its last. Nothing was queued, no retry followed, and that sender was never told their mail failed. The server recorded it as a report that went: no audit row, no error line, and no movement in the count of reports it owes. `blamepost queue remove` and the console queue page recorded the same cancellation as one whose sender had been written to. Such a report now files the same `blamepost.mail.delivery.report_unsent` row as a report a generation ceiling refused, names the refusal the outbound path gave, and is counted with them. A cancellation whose report could not leave answers `report-recorded-unsent` with `reported` false. A report that reached the outbound queue and is waiting for a retry is unaffected and is still counted as sent.

items.title: The outbound posture this server reports is the one it runs
items.body: `BLAMEPOST_OUTBOUND_POLICY` carries the MTA-STS posture and the DANE posture, and the two settings are independent, so naming one and leaving the other alone is ordinary. A configuration naming no `dane` value ran the shipped `opportunistic` and reported no DANE posture at all, so `blamepost doctor` and the administration console showed nothing in that field for a server that was applying it. Both values are now reported as the server resolved them.

items.title: The count of held-back images describes images that would load
items.body: A message is shown with its images held back and a line offering to show them, and the count in that line was taken from every `img` tag the message carried. A tag written inside an HTML comment, or one carrying only a source set, is dropped whether or not the reader asks for images, so a message whose only image was one of those offered a reader the choice and then showed them the page they already had. The count is now taken from the rendering the reader would get, and counts only images carrying a source, so the line appears when something is actually being withheld. An image carried inside the message still counts, because the reading default holds those back too.

items.title: A retention sweep no longer deletes a bundle that restores in order to keep one that does not
items.body: A bundle's manifest records the id it was written as, the data directory it was taken from and the server it was taken on, and `restore apply` refuses a bundle whose fields disagree with the server it is run on. `backup verify`, `backup inspect` and the `--keep` sweeps on `backup run` and `backup purge` read the same manifest and did not ask. So a directory copied to a second name in the storage directory verified, counted as one of the newest bundles to keep, and the sweep deleted the bundle it was a copy of; what survived was the one a restore refuses. The same held for a bundle recording another data directory or another hostname. All four verbs now read the manifest through one reader that answers where the bundle came from in the same call: `verify` refuses before it decrypts a file, `inspect` prints a `restores here` line and exits `1`, and a sweep leaves such a bundle in place and names it with the reason it was not counted.

items.title: The scratch space `backup verify` asks for covers every file it opens
items.body: `backup verify` decrypts every file a bundle holds into a temporary directory, and the free-space check it makes first counted only the files a restore would write. A bundle taken before the volume's reserved names were excluded carries the earlier volume's rollback directory under one of them, so the check could report enough room and the verify then run out of it. The check now measures the same set of files the run opens.

items.title: `queue list` screens the names of message bodies no descriptor accounts for
items.body: `queue list` names each message body in the spool that no descriptor accounts for, because clearing one takes its id. That id is the file's own name, and the list exists precisely because the file is one this server did not write, so the name had not been checked by anything. A name carrying U+009B opened an escape sequence in the operator's terminal and could erase the line it was printed on, which is the line saying why the queue reads as empty while mail is being refused. Those names now go through the same screen the rest of the operator surface uses, so the name is shown and the terminal does not act on it. Reaching this needs write access to the data volume.

items.title: Mail is refused for a mailbox whose erasure could not finish
items.body: `blamepost account remove --destroy` puts the account row out of service before it destroys anything, and it records that in two columns, because a records-retention posture can put a trigger on the status column and refuse the transition itself. The recipient lookup read the status column on its own. On a volume that refused that one write, the mailbox went on being a deliverable recipient while everything else treated it as erasing: `blamepost account list` showed it as `erasing`, every credential was refused at sign in, `blamepost account resume` refused it, and the mail exchanger still answered `250` for mail addressed to it. That mail was filed into a mailbox whose owner could no longer open it and whose remaining contents this server had been asked to destroy, and the sender was told it had arrived. Both columns are now read together wherever an account's state decides anything, so such a mailbox is answered `550 5.1.1 No mailbox by that name at this server.` at `RCPT TO`, and an alias forwarding into it reports the same for that recipient. An erasure on a volume that took both writes behaves as before.

items.title: `Email/get` reported every message as carrying no files
items.body: `hasAttachment` was `false` on every message the JMAP surface answered for, whatever the message carried. A client that filters or renders on it was told the whole mailbox was bare, including the messages whose own conversation page listed their files. RFC 8621 section 4.1.4 makes it true when the message has parts a client should offer as downloadable, and it is now read from the mark each message records. Run `blamepost attachments backfill` for the mail that was already on the volume; until that has run, those messages answer true, which is the answer that hides nothing.

items.title: A certificate watch asked for with a value that is not a boolean was turned off
items.body: `blamepost.tlsContext` accepted `watch` as anything and folded every value that was not the boolean `true` to off. `watch: "true"` and `watch: 1` each read as a request for the watch and each disabled it, so the process went on presenting the certificate it started with and a renewal written to the certificate files was never picked up, with nothing thrown and nothing logged. The option is now refused where it is accepted unless it is `true` or `false`.

items.title: A peer refused over DANE is now in the report its domain receives
items.body: A mail exchanger whose certificate matches none of the TLSA records its own domain publishes is refused, which RFC 7672 section 2.2 requires. That refusal was not recorded, so the daily TLS report this server sends that domain counted the attempt as neither a success nor a failure and the receiver saw nothing about it in the one place they would look. The attempt is now recorded as `validation-failure`, one of the result types RFC 8460 section 4.3 defines, and appears in the next report for that domain beside the mail exchanger it was made against. A TLSA lookup that could not complete under an enforcing posture was already reported as `dane-required` and is unchanged, and no delivery decision changes.

items.title: SECURITY.md now states the condition under which a release carries no post-quantum signature
items.body: The fourth verification recipe told operators that a missing `<tarball>.mldsa.sig` was expected when `keys/release-pqc-pub.json` was absent from the source at that tag. That public key is committed from v0.1.0 on, so the test it described answers for no release after it, while the publish workflow omits the signature whenever the release-signing secret is unset. An operator following the old text read a fetchable key beside a missing signature as unexplained. The recipe now names the secret as the condition, points at the warning annotation the publish run records, and says that a key which fetches is not evidence that a release was signed with it.

items.title: A delivery refused over an MTA-STS lookup sent operators to the wrong fault
items.body: Outbound mail under an enforcing MTA-STS posture is refused with status `5.7.10`, and its sender told, when the MTA-STS record lookup cannot complete. That reaches domains publishing no MTA-STS record at all, and the cause is this server's own outbound DNS rather than anything the destination published. The queue troubleshooting guidance read as though every MTA-STS failure belonged to the receiver, so an operator whose container had lost DNS was sent to contact destinations that were working. It now separates the two, quotes the reason text that tells them apart, and says to check outbound DNS with `blamepost doctor` before contacting a destination. Messages already refused this way have to be sent again once DNS is working.

items.title: `blamepost doctor` passed an SPF record every receiver refuses
items.body: RFC 7208 caps a published SPF record at 450 characters, and a receiver answers a longer one with a permanent error before it reads the policy in it, so the domain authorizes nobody however the record ends. The posture report read the policy and reported on that, so a domain whose record had grown past the cap was told its SPF was correct while its mail failed SPF everywhere. The report now reports the length and the cap, and names the two ways to get back under it. A domain that has been failing SPF for no visible reason is the case this finds.

items.title: `blamepost doctor --dane` counted TLSA records no sender is permitted to use
items.body: RFC 7672 §1.3 lets a sender authenticate a server against a TLSA record only when the DNS answer carrying it was DNSSEC-authenticated. The check counted the records and reported how many came back, so a zone publishing TLSA records with no DNSSEC over them read as a server that senders could authenticate, and no sender ever did. The check now reports whether the answer was authenticated. An unauthenticated answer is a failure naming both places it is fixed, the zone's signing or the resolver this server reads, and a resolver that reports neither leaves the row marked as one that could not be checked rather than as either verdict.

items.title: The closing line of `blamepost doctor` could name a FAIL it had not printed
items.body: The summary is written from two counts, the checks that disagreed and the records that could not be read. One of its arms said "Each FAIL above names one" in the case where the first count was zero, which sends a reader looking for a line that is not in the report. Each sentence is now written by the count it is about.

items.title: A posture report could leave out the DKIM rows and still say everything is in place
items.body: `blamepost.mail.posture.create` takes an optional DKIM handle, and leaving it out leaves the selector checks out of the report by design. A handle that was supplied and could not answer which selectors to expect took the same path, so the selector rows disappeared from a run that then closed by saying the zone matched. It is now refused where the checker is built, as is a resolver handle short of any reader the report calls, which previously reported those records as lookups that did not complete and sent the operator to a resolver nothing had asked.

items.title: `blamepost doctor` passed a DMARC record it could not read
items.body: This server reads a published DMARC record up to 4096 characters and treats a longer one as no policy at all, which is the answer every verdict resting on the record already reached. The zone report did not measure the length: it handed the record to the parser, printed what came back, and closed by calling the domain's DMARC posture correct. So one server held two opposite readings of one zone, and the lenient one was the report an operator runs to find out whether the zone is right. The report now refuses a record over the cap and names the length beside it. It does not quote the record back, because a record refused for its length is one no console should print whole.

items.title: A filter naming something this server cannot run is refused at upload
items.body:
A Sieve script declares the extensions it uses in a `require` line, and a script requiring one this server does not carry was already refused while its author was looking at the error. An action or a test written without that line is not declared, and the grammar takes it: `vacation`, `reject`, `ereject`, `addflag`, `notify` and a misspelling of `fileinto` all passed the check and were stored. The name was resolved at delivery instead, once per arriving message, and the refusal cost the whole script rather than the one line. Every rule in it stopped filing, every message fell through to INBOX, and the author had been told the upload succeeded.

`PUTSCRIPT` now answers `NO` for a script naming anything the filter cannot run, and `blamepost account sieve` and the browser interface refuse it the same way, quoting what could not be run. A refused upload leaves the stored script as it was, so an edit that would have stopped a working filter does not replace it. `redirect` is unaffected: the filter carries it, and a script using it is stored and runs.

items.title: A `fileinto` no longer loses to a `keep` written above it
items.body:
A message is filed once here, so a script naming two destinations gets one of them, and which one it got followed from the order the lines were written in. A `keep` above a `fileinto` took INBOX, the folder the script named received nothing, and no line anywhere said so. The folder the script names is now the one taken whichever line came first.

Every destination a script asks for and this server does not use is recorded under `blamepost.mail.sieve.action_unavailable` and written to the error log, which is the row a `redirect` this server cannot perform already recorded. A script writing `keep` and `discard` together still keeps the message, in both orders.

items.title: A filter rule written against an alias now matches
items.body:
RFC 5228 section 5.4 reads `envelope :to` as the address that caused the delivery, and this server handed the filter the mailbox behind that address instead. The two are the same string for mail sent straight to a mailbox and differ for every alias, so a rule of the form `if envelope :is "to" "sales@example.com" { fileinto "Sales"; }` matched nothing, filed nothing and recorded nothing, and mail to the alias arrived in INBOX alongside everything else. Filing by the address mail arrived at is what the test is for, since the messages carry the same `To` header either way. `envelope :to` is now the recipient the peer wrote in `RCPT TO`.

A rule testing `envelope :to` against a mailbox's own address is unchanged for mail addressed to that mailbox. It stops matching for mail that reached the mailbox through an alias, which is the address the message was not sent to; a rule meant to cover both names both addresses.

items.title: A TLS report no longer calls a policy invalid when the policy was never read
items.body: RFC 8461 gives one enhanced status to two different MTA-STS refusals: a policy this server could not fetch, and a policy whose mail exchanger list covers none of the domain's own. The aggregate TLS report sent to the receiving domain was keyed on that status alone, so both arrived as `sts-policy-invalid`. A domain whose policy is correct, and whose policy endpoint or `_mta-sts` record this server could not reach, was being told to go and change it. The two are now separated: a policy that could not be retrieved is reported as `sts-policy-fetch-error`, which RFC 8460 section 4.3 registers for exactly that, and a policy covering none of the domain's mail exchangers still reports `sts-policy-invalid`.

items.title: A delivery refused over DANE is reported under the receiver's TLSA records
items.body:
RFC 8460 section 4.4 spells that policy type `tlsa`, and these reports carried `no-policy-found`, which tells a domain running DANE that no policy was applied to the delivery its own records refused. Both DANE refusals now arrive under `tlsa`: TLSA records that were required and could not be obtained, and records that were obtained and matched none of the peer's certificate chain.

A report for one domain can now carry more than one policy entry, one per policy the period's attempts were judged under, which is what the `policies` array of the report format is for. A domain that publishes an MTA-STS policy and TLSA records reads each set of failures beside the document it is about. Nothing changes on the receiving side beyond that: publish `_smtp._tls` and the reports arrive as before.

items.title: A folder whose name carries a slash or a backslash could not be opened in the browser
items.body:
IMAP `CREATE` makes a mailbox at any depth, so an account can hold `Clients/Acme`, and the browser built that folder's link by percent-encoding the whole name into a path segment. A request path carrying an encoded separator or a null byte is answered `400 Bad Request` before any route matches it, so the folder was listed and answered nothing when it was opened. A name carrying a backslash failed the same way, because that character encodes to the other refused escape.

The folder now travels in the query string and both open. The request screening is unchanged, and a folder name is still screened before it is stored, so the characters that make one name render as another are still refused at `CREATE`.

items.title: JMAP reported every mailbox as sitting at the top of the tree
items.body:
`Mailbox/get` answered `parentId: null` on every mailbox and put the whole path in `name`, and the session document advertised `maxMailboxDepth` as `1`. An account holding `Clients/Acme` was drawn by a JMAP client as one mailbox named `Clients/Acme` beside the inbox, while an IMAP client on the same account showed it under `Clients`.

`parentId` now names the level above, `name` carries the last level alone as RFC 8621 section 2 requires, and every `parentId` in an answer names another mailbox in the same answer, which is what a client needs to draw the tree. A level that no mailbox of the account answers to, which is what IMAP `DELETE` leaves behind and lists as `\NonExistent \HasChildren`, is answered with every right false: it holds no message, nothing may be filed into it, and `Email/query` naming it matches nothing. `maxMailboxDepth` is now `null`, which RFC 8621 section 1.6.2 defines as no limit, because nothing here caps how many levels a name carries. What is capped is the length of a name, which `maxSizeMailboxName` reports, and the 1000 mailboxes one account may hold.

A mailbox id is still the full path, which is the value `Email/query` takes in `inMailbox`, so a client that stored ids keeps working. A client that cached the flat tree redraws it when it next fetches the mailbox list.

items.title: The mailbox page and the accounts page reported nothing stored
items.body:
Both read a quota by wire folder name, and a wire folder name belongs to every account that has one, so the reading could name no mailbox to measure and answered zero bytes, zero messages and no cap. The mailbox page showed `0 stored, 0 B` with a meter that never moved, and the accounts page showed the cap an operator had set with nothing beside it.

Both now read the account's own total, summed over every folder it owns, which is the same arithmetic the append path measures against the cap. The mailbox page reads `4 stored in this mailbox, 22 KB of 64 KB` and its meter reads that total against the cap; each accounts row reads the usage, the cap and the number of messages held. An account the operator left uncapped shows its usage and `No cap`. The counters come off the message store, so what is shown is what the volume holds.

items.title: Audit rows written on a mail connection carried no peer address
items.body:
SECURITY.md tells an operator to read the peer on the delivery and wire rows and the actor on the administrative ones. The mail listeners wrote neither: a refused IMAP `CREATE`, a denied expunge, a refused Sieve upload and a refused submission all landed with the peer column empty, so what else came from one address was not answerable from the trail.

Those rows now carry the address the connection came from, and the identifier of the connection beside it, so two sessions one account opened at once are told apart. Where the exchange proved an identity, the account or sending credential is on the row with the address. Where it proved none, the address stands alone: the name a refused attempt claimed is a name whoever is guessing chose, and it is not written into the column that answers who acted. A command-line invocation still carries no peer. `blamepost audit read` and `b.audit.query` filter on those columns, so a search by address now reaches the wire rows. Rows written before this release keep what they were given, because the trail is append-only.

items.title: The sign-in page said the page had been served over TLS
items.body: The line under the form read that the session cookie's `__Host-` prefix and `Secure` attribute mean the page is served over TLS. That is not true in a supported configuration: a host install accepts a password over the cleartext port from `127.0.0.1`, and the sentence told a reader on that connection that it was encrypted. The line now states the two cookie properties and nothing about the connection that carried the page.

items.title: POP3 sends a message with CRLF line endings and counts it that way
items.body: RFC 1939 section 3 sends every line of a message ending in CRLF. A message stored with a bare line feed, or with no line ending after its last line, now reaches a POP3 client with CRLF in each place, and the sizes `STAT` and `LIST` report count those octets, so a client that reads exactly the advertised count receives the whole message.

items.title: Publishing a TLSA record through the DNS writer was refused by the provider
items.body: The DNS writer sent a TLSA record with its value in `content`, and the provider takes a TLSA record's usage, selector, matching type and association data as separate fields, so a preview listed the record and the write was refused. The writer now sends the four fields, and reads them back to compare against what was written.

items.title: The DMARC policy step counted sampled or interrupted quarantine toward the hold before reject
items.body: The step to `p=reject` asks for 14 days at `p=quarantine`, measured from the policy observations this server records. A change from `pct=10` to full enforcement was not recorded as a change, so the days at 10 percent counted. A record that disappeared, or stopped being readable, was not recorded at all, so publishing quarantine again reused the date it was first seen. Both are now recorded, and the hold is measured from the start of the current run of full quarantine. A domain whose last recorded state was sampled or interrupted starts its hold again at the next reading.

items.title: Erasing a DMARC report contact no longer lets a resent report count twice
items.body: An erasure request for an address that an aggregate report names as its contact destroyed the report row and left its records, which still count toward the policy evidence. A resend of the same report was then stored as new, and its records counted a second time. The report row is now erased and written again without the contact address, with its records moved onto it, so a resend is still recognized as one and the address it carries is not stored again.

items.title: A DMARC percentage outside 0 to 100 was read as published
items.body: RFC 7489 section 6.3 makes `pct` a whole number from 0 to 100. A record carrying `pct=250`, `pct=1.5` or any other value outside that was reported as a published policy with that percentage. `blamepost.mail.posture.dmarcRecord` now reads such a record as unusable and names the value, as it does for a record that will not parse, so `blamepost dmarc preview` and the DMARC policy step in the admin console report it that way.

items.title: Text somebody else wrote no longer reaches a terminal as an escape sequence
items.body:
`blamepost account messages` prints the `From` and `Subject` of each message it lists, and a Sieve script that fails to parse is refused with the part of the script that failed quoted back. Both values are written by somebody other than the operator reading them. The screen in front of both removed the two-byte escape sequences but passed the single-byte forms in the U+0080 to U+009F range, of which U+009B is CSI: a terminal printing it acts on the rest of the line rather than showing it, so a subject could clear the row above it or repaint the `HELD` marker onto a message that does not carry one, on the listing an operator builds a preservation answer from. That range is now removed from both after the existing screen has run, and from the DMARC report identifiers the same listing prints. The text either value was carrying is still shown, so a record can still be matched by what it says; only the control characters are taken out, and the stored value is unchanged.

The browser pages are screened the same way, for the same reason: a page renders a control inertly, and the values on it are read again in the server log and in `blamepost audit read`. Message subjects, the account display names on the accounts page, the detail on each row of the audit page, and the record content a DNS provider returns on the zone confirmation page all have that range taken off. A tab in any of these values is shown as a space, since each is shown as one line. The accounts page and the audit page were not screening these values at all; they now use the same screen the rest of the interface uses.

That screen is now one reader rather than one per surface. The same one covers the message listing, the browser pages, the outbound queue that `blamepost queue list`, `blamepost queue show`, `blamepost queue held` and `blamepost queue flush` print, the zone diff `blamepost zone preview` prints, the findings `blamepost doctor` reports, and the text a DNS provider returns in a refusal. Alongside the tab, a carriage return and a line feed in any of those values are shown as a space, for the same reason the tab is: each value is shown on one line, and a line break in one turned a single row into what read as two. `blamepost audit read` screened none of these values and now screens the reason on each row and the resource it names, both of which quote whatever caused the event. The rows this server files when it could not send a delivery report carry the same screen on the address that was owed one and on the reason it was not sent, as do the rows recording a retry sweep or a TLS report run that ended in an error. The zone diff screens the record address and the record type beside the record value, all three of which come out of the provider's answer.

Audit rows carry that screen too, in the columns that say who acted. Two of the four are written from what a peer sent, and the reading in front of them cut each field at the first control character it found. That kept whatever came before it and dropped the rest, so a row lost the end of the value it was recording, while a bidirectional override or a zero-width character earlier in the same field went through untouched and a row could render as something other than what it says. Those fields now go through the same screen as every other displayed value: what a reader would act on is removed and the rest of the field is kept, so a value from a peer cannot reorder or hide part of a row, and a noisy agent string is recorded in full rather than truncated at its first control byte.

Two fields are refused on the way in rather than repaired on the way out, because they are stored once and shown repeatedly. An account display name carrying any control character is refused where the account is created or changed, from the console and from the API alike, and that now covers the U+0080 to U+009F range as well as the tab, the carriage return, the line feed and the rest of the C0 range. An aggregate DMARC report whose organization name or report identifier carries one is refused whole and nothing from it is stored, where previously such a report was taken and the name was left for each reader to deal with.

items.title: Every mailbox a From or Sender header names is measured against the account sending it
items.body: A `From` header naming two mailboxes, where the first was written as a bare address and the second in angle brackets, was measured only on the second. `From: colleague@example.com, Alice <alice@example.com>` was read as one mailbox whose display name happened to contain a colleague's address, so the first was never compared with the addresses the account holds or with a sending credential's refused local parts. The message was accepted, signed with the domain's DKIM key and relayed, and a receiver displayed both mailboxes. Each comma-separated piece of a `From` or `Sender` header that parses as an address on its own is now a mailbox in its own right and is measured like any other, and a message naming one the account may not write is answered `550 5.7.1`. A display name carrying a comma is unaffected: `From: Doe, John <john@example.net>` is still one mailbox, because `Doe` does not parse as an address. This applies to submission over SMTP, to the browser compose form and to JMAP `EmailSubmission/set`, which reach one implementation of the check.

items.title: An IMAP literal larger than the message ceiling is refused before any of it is read
items.body: The IMAP listener accepted a literal of up to 64 MiB whatever `maxMessageBytes` was set to, read all of it into memory, and then had the message store refuse the `APPEND`. A literal announcing more than `maxMessageBytes` is now answered `NO` with the ceiling named, and the continuation that invites its octets is not sent. The ceiling applies to every literal, including the ones `LOGIN`, `AUTHENTICATE` and `ID` may carry before a client has signed in, which on the shipped value of 50 MiB is the largest literal an unauthenticated connection can open.

items.title: A restore refuses a bundle whose manifest someone else signed
items.body: A manifest carries the public key its signature is checked under, so a signature that verified proved neither who wrote it nor that it was unchanged. Anyone who could write to the backup location could remove files from a manifest, sign it with a key of their own, and have `restore apply` put the result in place and report it verified. After moving a bundle into place, `restore apply` now compares the key that signed the manifest with the audit signing key sealed inside the bundle, which only the holder of both passphrases can read or replace, and puts the previous volume back when they differ. `backup inspect` and `backup verify` say that their signature line is not evidence of who signed without `--fingerprint`.

items.title: A restore refuses a renamed bundle, a bundle from another hostname, and a volume another process holds
items.body: `restore apply` refuses before anything moves when the bundle id recorded in the manifest is not the id it was asked for, which is what copying an older bundle under a newer name produces, and when the manifest records a different `BLAMEPOST_HOSTNAME` from the server's. It refuses when the filesystem holding the data directory has less free space than the bundle's decrypted files. `restore apply` and `restore rollback` take the data volume's lock and refuse with `store/volume-in-use` while another process holds it; both previously moved the files of a volume a running server was writing. `backup inspect` exits `1` for a bundle whose recorded id differs from its name.

items.title: A restore says how far it rewinds
items.body: The report from `restore apply` names the moment the bundle was taken, the key that signed it, the audit trail counter the replaced volume had been anchored at beside the bundle's, and how many bundles in storage are newer than the one restored. `--json` carries the same values as `bundleCreatedAt`, `signedBy`, `replacedAnchor`, `restoredAnchor` and `newerBundles`. A restore from an older bundle brings back credentials and accounts revoked or removed since it was taken, and those lines are how an operator sees it before starting the server.

items.title: A sending credential is refused an operator mailbox created after it was issued
items.body: A sending credential refuses `postmaster`, `abuse` and every mailbox in its domain carrying the operator role, and the operator mailboxes were read once, when the credential was issued. A mailbox created with the operator role, or given the role from the console, after that moment could be written as by every credential already issued for its domain, as the envelope sender and as the `From` author, over submission and over `POST /api/send`. The server now reads the operator role from the account each time it checks a sender or an author, so that mailbox is refused from the next message, including on a submission session that authenticated before the change. The refusal applies whatever the credential's own list holds: `blamepost credential refusals <id> --clear` still permits `postmaster` and `abuse` and leaves every operator mailbox refused. For a credential to write as an operator mailbox, take the operator role away from the account, and take the local part off the credential's list if the list names it. No credential needs to be reissued.

items.title: The browser does not keep a copy of a page behind a session
items.body: Every page served to a signed-in account carries `Cache-Control: private, no-store`: the mailbox, a message, compose, search, every administration page, a confirmation page, an error page and a reference page. The sign-in page carries it too, and so does the 426 answer to a GET on `/jmap/ws` that asks for no WebSocket upgrade. These responses carried `private, no-cache, must-revalidate`, which RFC 9111 lets a browser store and reuse after asking the server again, so a message a reader opened could stay in that browser's disk cache after they signed out, on a shared or public machine as well as their own. The front page and the reference pages served to a visitor with no session keep `private, max-age=900`. A copy a browser stored under an earlier version stays in its cache until the browser evicts it or the reader clears it.

items.title: A page template writes the leading slash of every link it renders
items.body: Every link and form target in the web interface and the reference wiki is written in its page template as a slash followed by the rest of the path. The server builds that remainder with one function per surface, which checks that the whole path is on this server and throws when the remainder begins with a slash, a backslash, a tab, a line feed or a carriage return. The browser reads anything placed after the template's slash as a path on this server, including a value that begins `javascript:`, `data:` or `https:`. The addresses the pages link to are unchanged, and there is nothing to configure.

items.title: Account passwords and the sealed volume run on the corrected Argon2
items.body: The new floor carries the Argon2 validation fix Node shipped in 24.20.0. Argon2id hashes every account password and derives the key that seals the data volume from `BLAMEPOST_VAULT_PASSPHRASE`, so both run on the corrected code from this release forward. Stored hashes keep their existing format, and no password or passphrase needs to be changed.

items.title: The runtime carries the fix for the Brotli decoder flaw CVE-2026-111497
items.body:
CVE-2026-111497, published under the name Node2Shell, is an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder that Node uses for `zlib` Brotli decompression. Node rates it High, and crafted compressed input can lead to code execution in the Node process. Node 24.22.1 and Node 26.12.1 carry the fix, along with six other CVEs in `tls`, `dns`, `http`, `crypto` and the permission model.

The new floor is 24.22.1. The container image is built on base images that run Node 26.12.1 on both `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`. That runtime links the system libbrotli rather than Node's bundled copy, and the image carries libbrotli 1.2.1, the upstream release that fixes the same CVE.

This server decompresses gzip and zip report attachments and does not decode Brotli from any peer, so no path in this server reaches the flawed decoder.
