The runtime is upgraded regardless, because the same release fixes the TLS and DNS input handling that every listener and every outbound delivery relies on. A host install needs Node 24.22.1 or newer; the container image needs no change from the operator.

items.title: A SHAKE256 digest that cannot allocate its output reports the failure
items.body: An allocation failure inside a SHAKE256 extendable-output digest is handled and reported instead of going unchecked. SHAKE256 derives the keys that seal storage and hashes sending-credential secrets, so a failure on either path surfaces as an error rather than as a value.

items.title: OpenSSL 3.5.8, and root certificates from NSS 3.126
items.body: The floor brings OpenSSL 3.5.8 and the root certificate set from NSS 3.126, which is what outbound SMTP and every HTTPS request this server makes verify a peer against. It also brings Node's handling of an incomplete RSA private key and the clearing of provider-side copies of private key material, which is the path the RSA half of a DKIM selector signs on.

items.title: A reporting organization is counted by the domain that authenticated its reports
items.body: The DMARC policy step to `p=quarantine` asks for reports from two organizations, and the step to `p=reject` asks for three. The server counted an organization by the `<org_name>` value in each report, which the sender writes. One sender that passed DMARC for one domain could send reports under three names, count as three organizations and supply the aligned volume as well, and `blamepost dmarc status` and the DMARC console then offered `p=reject` on reports that sender wrote. An organization is now the registered domain that the message carrying its reports passed DMARC for. One domain counts once whatever names its reports use, the subdomains of one registered domain count once, and a party that holds several registered domains counts once per domain. `blamepost reports list`, `blamepost reports show` and the DMARC console show that domain as the organization and print the `<org_name>` value beside it as the name the reports give. A report stored under another reporter's name and report id no longer stops that reporter's own report from being stored, unless both reports passed DMARC for the same registered domain. The first boot of this version adds a column to the aggregate report table and replaces the table's unique index. Reports stored before the upgrade count toward no organization and their messages stay in the totals, so the organization count for a domain starts from the reports that arrive after the upgrade. There is nothing to configure.

items.title: The JMAP WebSocket accepts a browser only from this server's HTTPS origins
items.body: An upgrade at `/jmap/ws` compared the host in the browser's `Origin` header with the `Host` header and ignored the scheme, so a page served over cleartext at `http://<BLAMEPOST_HOSTNAME>` passed the check against a server that serves the web interface over TLS. The upgrade now accepts `https://<BLAMEPOST_HOSTNAME>` and, when this process holds the certificate, `https://<BLAMEPOST_HOSTNAME>:<BLAMEPOST_HTTPS_PORT>`, and refuses every other `Origin` with `403` and an audit row under `blamepost.jmap.websocket.refused`. A client that sends no `Origin` header is accepted when it carries a session. If a proxy publishes the web interface under another name or port, a browser JMAP client there cannot open the socket, and `POST /jmap/api` and `/jmap/eventsource` still answer it.

items.title: A JMAP submission's envelope sender is bound to the account
items.body: `EmailSubmission/set` ignored `envelope`: the message left from the account's own address to the draft's `To` addresses whatever `mailFrom` and `rcptTo` named. `envelope.mailFrom` must now be an address `Identity/get` lists for the account. Any other address is refused `forbiddenMailFrom` and recorded under `blamepost.web.author_not_permitted` with surface `jmap-submission-envelope`; the submission port checks `MAIL FROM` against the same set. `envelope.rcptTo` is the recipient list. It must name every `To` and `Cc` address of the draft, each address it adds is sent as a blind copy, and it may name at most 100 recipients. SMTP parameters on `mailFrom` or on a recipient are refused `invalidProperties`.

items.title: JMAP advertises its request limits and refuses a request past one
items.body: The session document carried an empty `urn:ietf:params:jmap:core` capability, and `Email/get`, `Email/set` and the other methods took any number of ids, looking each one up in every folder of the account with an audit row for each lookup. The capability now carries `maxSizeRequest` 10485760, `maxCallsInRequest` 32, `maxConcurrentRequests` 4, `maxObjectsInGet` 500, `maxObjectsInSet` 500, `maxSizeUpload` 1, `maxConcurrentUpload` 1 and an empty `collationAlgorithms`, which are the framework's strict JMAP profile. A `/get` call naming more than 500 ids and a `/set` call naming more than 500 objects are refused `requestTooLarge`. The same 10 MiB is the JSON body limit of every route, including `/api/send`. A fifth request to `POST /jmap/api` from an account that already has four open is refused `400` with the `limit` problem type.

items.title: A browser session ends when its account's domain is disabled
items.body: An account on a disabled domain could not sign in, and a browser session it already held kept working: its webmail, its JMAP session and, for an administrator, the whole admin console answered as before until the session expired. Every browser request now reads the account's domain as well as the account, and a session whose domain is disabled or no longer hosted is sent to `/sign-in`, or answered `401` on JMAP, at its next request. Disabling a domain from the console is refused when it would leave no administrator able to sign in, as before.

items.title: The account creation form no longer grants the operator role
items.body: The form that creates an account carried a checkbox that created the account holding the operator role. That grant asked for no reason and filed only `account.created`, so it did not appear under `account.role_granted`. The checkbox is gone, and a creation request naming `isAdmin` is refused `400` and creates nothing. Give an existing account the role with Give it the console on its row, which asks for a reason. To find administrators created through the checkbox, run `blamepost audit read --action account.created` and read the rows whose metadata carries `isAdmin` set to true.

items.title: A signing key that is not the one its selector publishes refuses instead of signing
items.body: Every sealed private key is now checked against the public half its own selector record carries before it signs anything. A `keys` folder and a database restored from different points in time leave a key file that opens and parses under a record carrying a different key, and every reading this server offers answers off the record, so `blamepost dkim records`, the admin interface and the `signing keys` line of `blamepost doctor` all reported the domain correct while its signatures failed at every receiver. The domain now sends unsigned and says so, with the selector named in the server log and a row under `blamepost.mail.listeners.submission_unsigned`. Restore the volume from a backup whose `keys` folder and `db.enc` were taken together, or run `blamepost dkim retire` followed by `blamepost dkim generate` and publish both records it prints.

items.title: Each DKIM private key is sealed to the selector it belongs to
items.body:
A private key in the `keys` folder was sealed to the data volume and to nothing else, so every sealed value that volume held opened in place of every other: a file put under a selector's name opened as that selector's signing key whatever it had been sealed as, and a key pair copied in from another hosted domain together with the selector records naming it signed for the domain it was copied onto. Each key is now sealed to its domain, selector and algorithm. A value sealed as anything else is refused with `example.com cannot sign, because the signing key for its 'bp202608' selector (ed25519) is sealed, and not as this selector's signing key`, and the domain sends unsigned and files a row rather than signing something a receiver resolved the wrong key for.

Keys already on a volume carry the older seal. Stop the server and run `blamepost dkim reseal` once after upgrading; `--domain example.com` limits it to one domain. It opens each key, checks it against the public half its own selector record publishes, and writes it back sealed to that record, leaving the key material, the selector records and the zone unchanged. It is safe to run again, a run cut off part way is finished by running it again, and a key it will not rewrite is named and left exactly as it was found. The server signs throughout: a key the run has not reached is opened and checked against its own record exactly as a sealed-to-selector one is. The run records `blamepost.mail.dkim.keys_resealed`, naming who ran it, the domain and each selector whose key was rewritten.

items.title: A DKIM key-lifecycle row no longer carries text that redraws the terminal it is read in
items.body: The rows under `blamepost.mail.dkim.keys_generated`, `keys_rotated`, `keys_retired` and `selectors_swept` quote the selector name a command was given, and a refused name is whatever was typed. Control characters were removed from those values; a bidirectional override and a zero-width character were not, so a name carrying one reordered or hid the rest of the line in `blamepost audit read`. Both are removed now, through the same screen every other operator-facing value goes through. The audit chain is append-only, so rows written before this release keep whatever they were given.

items.title: A request the web interface cannot answer no longer returns the server's stack
items.body: The answer to a fault carried the exception's stack whenever `NODE_ENV` was anything other than `production`, and the stack names the absolute path of the directory this server was installed into and the source file the fault came from. The published container image sets `NODE_ENV=production`; a host running `blamepost serve` from a service unit or a shell sets nothing, so the disclosing answer was the default on every install that is not the image. Reaching it needed no account and no session: a request whose target is longer than 8192 characters is refused where the router parses it, before the session is read and before any route matches, and a visitor on the cleartext port received the stack. Every fault is now answered with its refusal code and nothing else, whatever the environment says. The whole stack is still written to the server's error log, which is where it was always meant to be read.

items.title: The recipient list, the sender's address and the message preview are screened before a reader sees them
items.body: A message's subject and the sender's display name were passed through the screen that removes bidirectional overrides, zero-width characters and control characters. Three values on the same rows were not: the recipient list under the sender's name on the conversation page, the bare address beside it, and the one-line preview in the folder list. A sender could therefore write a `To` header reading `quarterly gpj.exe` and have it shown as `quarterly exe.jpg` to the account holder deciding whether the message was addressed to them. All three now go through the same screen as the subject. The message body is still rendered exactly as it was written, so an emoji sequence and a Devanagari conjunct survive; the address a reply is sent to is also unchanged, because the screen is on the reading rather than on the value.

items.title: File names read off the data volume are screened before they reach a terminal
items.body: `blobs report` names every file under `blobs/` that is not a sealed body at the path its own digest gives, and `doctor` names every file in the key directory that no selector record claims and every spooled body with no descriptor. Each of those lists exists because the file is one the server did not write, so the name is not a value it validated. The names went to the terminal unscreened, and a name carrying U+009B followed by `2K` erases the line it is printed on: the line erased is a finding in the report written to say what is wrong with the volume. All three now go through the same screen the rest of this server prints through, which removes bidirectional overrides, invisible formatting characters and the C0 and C1 control ranges. The names on disk are unchanged, and the comparison that decides which key files no record claims still runs on the stored name.

items.title: A sender cannot write this server's own Authentication-Results header
items.body: This server writes an `Authentication-Results` header naming itself on every message it accepts, carrying the SPF, DKIM, DMARC and ARC results it computed, and RFC 8601 section 5 has a receiver remove any header already claiming that name before adding its own. The removal matched the field name as a literal line prefix. Three spellings that every RFC 5322 parser reads as the same header went past it: one folded onto a continuation line, one naming the server in a quoted string, and one with a space or a tab between the field name and its colon. A message arriving with any of those reached the mailbox carrying two verdicts under this server's name, one of them written by the sender, and a recipient's Sieve script testing `header :contains "Authentication-Results"` read the sender's. A message forwarded on by an alias carried it to the next receiver as well. Every `Authentication-Results` header claiming this server's name is now removed except the one this server wrote, read the way the parser that feeds Sieve reads it. On a message this server authenticated nothing about, which is one an account submitted and one whose authentication could not be completed and was accepted under `onTemperror: "accept"`, every such header is removed. Headers naming any other receiver are a previous hop's record and are left alone, and the rest of the message is unchanged byte for byte.

items.title: Each stored message body is sealed to the message it belongs to
items.body:
A message body under `blobs/` was sealed to the data volume and to nothing else, so every sealed value that volume held opened in place of every other. A body has a second thing placing it that a key does not: the file name is the SHA3-512 of the octets, and the read hashes what it opened back against that name, so a value that is not the message the row points at is refused rather than served. That check is unchanged and still runs.

What the seal adds is the order. Each body is now sealed under the name it is filed as, so a value sealed as something else is refused before its plaintext is produced, and the octets of another secret are not decoded and hashed inside the read serving a mailbox. The refusal reads `the stored body for message 3a7f... is sealed, and not as this message's body`, which says the file holds the wrong kind of value. The reading that follows a damaged body still sends an operator to restore the volume, and the two are now told apart in the report as well as at the read.

Bodies already on a volume carry the older seal and are read exactly as they were. There is no migration to run and no verb to run it: the file name places a body whatever form it is sealed in, and rewriting every body on a volume would put a write over files several accounts' rows already point at for a guard those rows already have. New bodies are 2256 bytes smaller each, because the seal they carry derives its key from the volume's own root instead of carrying a key encapsulation of its own, and `blobs report --verify` reads both forms.

items.title: An aggregate report counts as evidence when this server authenticated the message that carried it
items.body: A DMARC aggregate report is a document anybody who can reach your `rua=` address can compose, so a report counts toward the reading `blamepost reports` answers only where the message that carried it passed DMARC for the reporting organization. This server decides that by reading the `Authentication-Results` header its own inbound path wrote, and it read the `header.from` property of that header as a domain while the header carries the whole author address. No value the inbound path writes could be read, so every report that arrived was marked `carrier-domain-unreadable` and left out. `blamepost reports list` and the console reported nothing until `--include-unauthenticated` was passed, and a report from a reporter with a correct posture was indistinguishable from one a stranger sent. The property is now read in either spelling: the whole address, which is what this server writes, and the bare domain, which is what the RFC 8601 registry entry for the `dmarc` method defines and what another receiver may write. A value carrying more than one `@` names no party and is still refused. Reports already stored keep the mark they were filed with; a report that arrives after the upgrade is counted. Nothing about which reports are stored changes, and a report whose carrier did not authenticate is still kept, still marked, and still left out of the narrow reading.

items.title: A message could leave without asking for REQUIRETLS while the posture asking for it was on
items.body: `BLAMEPOST_REQUIRE_TLS` is the RFC 8689 posture every outbound envelope asks its receiver for, and a message may carry a posture of its own that wins over it. The server-wide setting has always been refused unless it is `true` or `false`. The per-message one was refused for nothing, and every value except `true` was read as the posture being off. A message carrying such a value went out with no REQUIRETLS keyword on its `MAIL FROM` line while the posture was on, was accepted by the receiver, and left nothing in the queue, the log or the audit trail saying the request had never been made. A per-message posture that is not `true` or `false` is now refused before the message reaches a socket, and the refusal names the setting. A message's place in the retry budget is read the same way: a value that was not a whole count either ended the message on its first attempt and told its sender it had failed, or left it with no wait between attempts so the receiver was offered it again on every sweep of the queue. No configuration file, environment variable or command line was affected, and no posture written by an operator changed.

items.title: An arriving DMARC report was held to the size bound only when it arrived as a gzip
items.body: A report reaches this server as an attachment somebody else composed, and the reader bounds what a container may carry before any of it is expanded. The bound was applied on the gzip path alone. An archive was opened under its entry count, its per-entry size and its expansion ratio, and under nothing that measured the archive itself, so a sender who chose ZIP was held to the carrier message ceiling instead and an operator who lowered the container bound read a figure that was true of one container and not of the other. The bound is now spent where the two paths are still one, so it holds whichever container the report arrives in, and a container over it is refused under `container-too-large` with the size recorded in the audit trail.

items.title: A mail session already open is refused once the account leaves service
items.body:
Suspending an account, archiving it, erasing it or withdrawing its domain reached the browser, JMAP and the admin console at the next request, and reached nothing else. A client holding an authenticated IMAP, POP3 or ManageSieve session kept fetching mail, and a submission session kept relaying it. An account suspended because its password had been taken went on serving every client that was already connected until those connections happened to close.

Each of the four listeners now re-reads the account and its domain on every command a signed-in session sends. IMAP, POP3 and ManageSieve answer the protocol's own negative verdict and the submission listener refuses the next message with `550 5.7.1`, and the refusal records which state stopped it, so a suspension, an archive, an erasure, a domain this server no longer hosts, a domain that is disabled and a row this server could not read are told apart. Each refusal writes an audit row under `blamepost.mail.listeners.session_account_stopped` naming the account, the address, the reason and the command that was being served. `CAPABILITY`, `NOOP` and `LOGOUT` are still answered, because they reach no mail.

Inbound mail is unaffected: a message for a mailbox out of service is decided at `RCPT` as before, and a composition that binds port 25 alone reaches none of this. The account is read per command rather than cached, so a change takes effect at the next command rather than at the end of a window.

Containment is now the same on every protocol: suspend the account, or disable the domain to reach every account on it at once.

items.title: A password is taken only over a connection this server can establish is encrypted
items.body:
The sign-in form accepted a posted password over the cleartext port from any peer, minted a session cookie carrying `Secure` and the `__Host-` prefix, and returned it on a cleartext response, which a browser discards under RFC 6265bis section 4.1.3. The password crossed an unprotected wire and the reader was returned to an empty form.

A credential is now taken when the socket is TLS, when the peer is loopback, or when a proxy named in `BLAMEPOST_TRUSTED_PROXIES` says the browser's connection was. Nothing else is accepted, and that setting holds nothing by default. Over a connection that carries none of those, `GET /sign-in` renders no password field at all and answers `403` with the reason, so the credential is not asked for before it is refused, and a session token replayed over the same connection is refused too.

What an operator needs to do depends on the deployment. The published image forwards a port into the container's own network namespace, so a request the host sends to `127.0.0.1` arrives from the bridge gateway and is refused a password like any other off-machine peer: use the TLS port. Behind a terminator, set `BLAMEPOST_TRUSTED_PROXIES` to the terminator's address range, which is also what makes the CSRF cookie carry `Secure`, the origin cross-check build its baseline as `https` and HSTS be sent. A host install reached from a browser on the same machine needs nothing. `X-Forwarded-Proto` from a peer no range names is ignored.

items.title: The words of a refusal reach a client screened, on every surface that hands one back
items.body:
A fault the web interface could not avoid was quoted back in several places with nothing taken off it: the `description` of a JMAP `SetError`, the `detail` of the `application/problem+json` answer the API returns, the scope line on the compose page, and the server's own log. One of those values is the name of a key off the caller's own JSON body, quoted twice by the shape reader when a request names a key it does not know, so a caller chose the codepoints. HTML escaping does not help: a bidirectional override and the single-byte control sequence introducer change what a terminal or a reader displays without being markup.

Every one of those values now goes through the same screen the rest of this server displays stranger text with, applied where the value is built rather than at each place it is written out, because one fault's words go to a log line, an audit row, a rendered page and a client's own display. An address a request asked to write as, quoted back into the refusal and into the audit row that records it, is screened after its length bound rather than before, so the ceiling stays on what the caller sent.

items.title: The payload of a refused literal is no longer read as commands
items.body:
A client sends a `{N+}` literal's payload without waiting for an answer, so when ManageSieve or IMAP refused the announcement, the payload was already on the wire and the listener read it line by line as commands. A ManageSieve `PUTSCRIPT` announcing more octets than the script ceiling could carry a line such as `DELETESCRIPT "name"`, and that line ran with the authority of the authenticated session. A SASL initial response sent as a literal for a mechanism the listener does not offer was quoted back in the refusal and in the log beside it.

Where the listener can tell how many octets follow, it now discards them: a `PUTSCRIPT` before authentication and an `AUTHENTICATE` naming an unoffered mechanism each draw one refusal. Where the wire guard refuses the announcement itself, the listener answers the refusal, then `BYE`, and closes the connection. A client that uses synchronizing `{N}` literals is refused before it sends any payload and keeps its connection.

releases.headline: A self-hosted mail server that runs as one container
releases.summary: blamepost serves SMTP, IMAP, JMAP, POP3, ManageSieve and a browser interface from a single process against a single data volume. Mail arrives over SMTP, is authenticated at DATA, filtered by the recipient's Sieve script, and is readable over IMAP, JMAP and POP3 or in the browser. Mail leaves over one policy chain that resolves the receiver, enforces MTA-STS, classifies what the far side said, retries on its own schedule and reports a permanent failure back to the account that sent it. There are no npm runtime dependencies: the framework it composes is vendored in the tarball you install. Read ROADMAP.md before deploying: it marks every capability shipped, targeted, accepted or under design, and it ships in that tarball beside the README.

items.title: One process, every protocol an operator's clients speak
items.body: Port 25 accepts inbound mail, 587 and 465 accept authenticated submission over STARTTLS and implicit TLS, 143 serves IMAP4rev2, 4190 serves ManageSieve, and 8080 and 8443 serve the browser interface, the administration surface and JMAP. POP3 on 110 is off unless you turn it on. Every mail listener requires TLS and none has a plaintext mode, so the server refuses to start without a certificate and key. The browser port on 8080 is the one that stays cleartext, because it is what a container health check and a proxy in front poll, and a session is not reachable over it: the session cookie is only ever sent back over TLS. Nothing binds 993 or 995: IMAP and POP3 negotiate TLS in band here, and a terminator in front of 143 or 110 does not stand in for that, because the listener is handed an unencrypted connection and refuses every credential offered over it. Port 25 does not bind while no domain is hosted, so a server that is running but not yet configured does not answer for recipients it knows nothing about, and the reason it declined is in the log and in the audit trail; the mailbox listeners and the browser interface come up regardless, which is how you finish the setup. An unacknowledged DNS posture is the stronger refusal and stops the whole boot rather than one listener, so BLAMEPOST_DNS_ACKNOWLEDGED and each hosted domain's own acknowledgment come before anything serves at all. Turning the MX listener off is the one setting that skips that question, because then nothing is accepting mail for the records to answer for. Each listener's port is individually overridable, which is how you run it behind standard host ports without giving the process any Linux capability. So are the ceilings every listener holds against one source address: how many connections that address may hold at once, and the connection, authentication-failure and refused-recipient rates. The largest message accepted is settable beside them and bounds one message rather than one address: the two SMTP listeners advertise it to senders as the SIZE keyword of RFC 1870 and refuse a larger one on the wire, and a mailbox refuses to store one however it got there, so an IMAP APPEND and a JMAP create meet the same number. That one lowers and does not raise. A stored message is written as one sealed file and the seal puts base64 inside base64, so the file is sixteen ninths of the message: 50 MiB of mail is an 89 MiB file, against the 96 MiB the read path serving IMAP BODY[] will open, and a higher setting would store messages nothing can fetch back. The defaults suit a peer delivering mail rather than a mailbox client, and the operator guide explains which one to raise when your users sit behind a single address.

items.title: Inbound mail is authenticated before it is accepted
items.body: SPF, DKIM verification, DMARC and the ARC chain all run at DATA, and the verdict is written into the Authentication-Results header your clients and filters read. HELO discipline and forward-confirmed reverse DNS run at the connection. Every one of those lookups goes through the one resolver this server holds rather than each gate building its own, so the connection checks and the message checks read a single view of the zone instead of two that can disagree. That resolver is built with the strict profile, which decides how an answer is parsed and bounded rather than where the question goes. Where it goes is the vendored framework's default, a public DNS-over-HTTPS endpoint. No setting here names a different one: neither the configuration file nor any BLAMEPOST_ variable reaches it, and the only substitution available is passing `blamepost.create` a resolver of your own, which means embedding this server rather than running the image. So every SPF, DKIM, DMARC and HELO lookup this server makes leaves the machine to that endpoint, and that endpoint sees every name a peer causes this server to ask about. It is the same resolver you are vouching for when you set `outboundPolicy.dnssecValidated: true` so `dane: "enforce"` will run. A domain that publishes no policy is scored as having no policy, not as a temporary DNS failure, so mail from it is not deferred at the wire.

items.title: Submission is bound to the authenticated identity
items.body:
An account may only send as an address it owns. A MAIL FROM for anything else is refused with 553 5.7.1 before a single recipient is accepted, and the session survives the refusal so a client that guesses wrong once can correct itself. This is not a policy option. An authenticated account that could send as any address is an open relay with extra steps.

The address a person actually reads is bound as well. Every address this server hosts, whether it is named in the From header or in a Sender header, has to be one the account may write: its own address, or an alias that points at it, with a subaddress tag folding to the address it extends. Where a message names several authors, every one of them at a domain this server hosts has to qualify, since a list mixing your address with a colleague's is the forgery rather than an exception to it, and at least one of the addresses named has to be yours. An author at a domain hosted elsewhere is left alone, so writing on behalf of an outside correspondent still works: this server's key creates no alignment for a domain it does not host, and that domain's own policy answers for it. A message carrying no From header, or a second From or Sender header, is refused whatever it names. Refusals happen before the message is signed, and the audit trail carries the identity that was rejected alongside the ones that would have been accepted. The client is answered permanently, so a conforming sender bounces the message to whoever wrote it instead of retrying one that will be refused identically until its queue lifetime runs out. Which permanent reply it gets says what to do about it: 550 5.7.1 means the header is well formed and names an address this account does not hold, which you grant as an alias or the writer stops claiming; 550 5.6.0 means the header block could not be read as a single author, which the sending client has to correct. The full explanation, naming the rejected address and the ones that would have been accepted, is in the log and the audit row rather than on the wire.

items.title: Sending credentials for an application that writes as a whole domain
items.body:
An account sends as one address. An application that sends under many local parts of one domain would otherwise need an account and a mailbox for each of them. A sending credential is the other shape: one secret scoped to one hosted domain, permitted to send as every local part in it and holding no mailbox at all. `blamepost credential add` issues one and records a reason; `blamepost credential list`, `blamepost credential show` and `blamepost credential bounces` read them back and answer while the server runs; and `blamepost credential rotate`, `blamepost credential revoke`, `blamepost credential remove` and `blamepost credential refusals` change one, each with a recorded reason. Revoke stops a credential and keeps its row, so the identifier on every audit row it produced still resolves; remove takes the row as well and needs `--destroy` beside the reason, the way erasing an account does.

The token reaches the terminal and nowhere else. The volume holds a digest of it, so no verb returns it and no audit row carries it, and a token that has been lost is replaced by rotating rather than read back. That is the opposite exposure from `blamepost zone token set`, which reads its token from a file because a command line is in the shell history and the process list. Here the value is one this server has just generated, so it has to come out somewhere, and the command says that this terminal and its scrollback are where it is exposed.

Bounces come back to a return path of the credential's own, `bounces+<id>@<domain>`, which is the address to put in the envelope sender of everything it sends. The domain carries one alias at `bounces@<domain>` pointing at a mailbox you name when the credential is issued, and that mailbox has to exist and be in service before anything is written. Leave `bounces@<domain>` free: something already standing there that delivers somewhere else refuses the whole call and names both addresses, and withdrawing the last credential in a domain takes the alias away again when this server was what wrote it. A bounce mailbox archived a month later leaves the credential working and every bounce refused at the door, so the return path is resolved on every read and `blamepost credential bounces` reports each credential that has stopped receiving.

Each credential carries two ceilings over a rolling window, one on messages and one on recipients, because a hundred messages carrying one recipient each and one message carrying a hundred thousand are different events and the second is what a stolen credential produces. Both are finite whether or not you name them. It also carries a list of local parts it refuses, which starts as `postmaster`, `abuse` and every mailbox in the domain holding the operator role. That list is replaced whole rather than added to, and emptying it opens up every address in the domain, so that one takes `--confirm` on top of the reason while naming the list does not. The counters the ceilings are measured against live in the process that is sending, so no command prints them and a restart puts every one of them back to zero.

Nothing on the wire accepts a credential in this release. The registry, the command line, the audit trail and the bounce routing are here, and the submission listener authenticates accounts and nothing else, so an application presenting a credential to 587 or 465 is refused as it would be without one. Issue them once the listener takes them. That same change is where `bounces` joins the list a credential refuses by default, since the list has to be enforced against the address a message claims to be written by before it can name the local part of the credential's own return path.

items.title: Sieve runs at delivery, and scripts are managed over ManageSieve
items.body: The recipient's active script runs against every message that arrives for them, from a peer and from a local sender alike, under a gas budget so a pathological script cannot burn delivery-path processor time without bound. A script is validated before it is stored. Actions that would put a message on the wire keep the message and record the refusal instead of dropping it, so the account holder still gets their mail and you can see what was asked for and not done. Scripts are uploaded, listed, fetched, renamed, activated and deleted over ManageSieve on 4190. `blamepost account sieve` reads what an account holds; it takes a reason and records that an administrator opened somebody's filter, so it is one of the verbs that needs the server stopped. The browser interface does not edit them, so an account holder who wants filtering needs a ManageSieve client.

items.title: One deletion path, with a retention floor and legal hold in front of it
items.body: IMAP EXPUNGE, the POP3 QUIT that applies a session's DELEs, JMAP Email/set destroyed and the browser interface's own purge all route through the same gate, so a message refused on one surface is refused on all of them, an account erasure included. Set BLAMEPOST_COMPLIANCE_POSTURE to soc2 for a one year floor below which a hard delete is refused, for the account owner as much as for an administrator, measured from the moment this server filed the message rather than from any date a client supplied with it. A message under legal hold survives regardless: the client is not told it went, a later session still finds it, and the body is still readable. With no posture set the floor is zero and legal hold is the only thing that keeps a message, which is what most operators want.

items.title: IMAP search answers or refuses, and never returns an empty set it cannot stand behind
items.body: A client searching a mailbox gets a real answer for the keys this server can evaluate: flags and keywords, arrival dates, sizes, sequence and identifier sets, subject, sender, the To addresses, the header fields it stores, and any boolean combination of those, matching on substrings as the specification requires rather than on whole words. For a key it cannot evaluate it refuses and names the key: the Cc and Bcc addresses, the body and whole-message keys, and the dates a message says it was sent on, as against the dates it arrived on. That property matters more than the list does. A search that quietly returns nothing tells the account holder their mailbox has no matches, and leaves them no way to discover the question was never asked. Most of the keys that refuse are the ones whose data this server does not keep, and every refusal names the key and says why. A HEADER key naming a field the store does not keep refuses the same way the named keys do, and so does a charset this server cannot read a term in. One limit is not about stored data at all: the extended result form RETURN asks for is not served, on either spelling of the command. A second one is about how a term arrives rather than what it asks. A term carried as a literal reaches the search on SEARCH and is dropped on UID SEARCH, so the UID form answers BAD because the key it was written for has nothing after it. A client sending a non-ASCII term usually sends it as a literal and usually asks for the UID form, so the two meet: write such a term inline until the framework's UID dispatch carries a literal through to the handler.

items.title: POP3 gives the maildrop to one session at a time and releases it when that session ends
items.body: RFC 1939 allows one session per maildrop, so this server hands it to whoever opens it first and refuses everybody else until that session is finished. Every way a session can finish releases it: a QUIT, the ten-minute idle close, or a link that dropped without either. So a client whose connection died reconnects and collects its mail rather than waiting out a timer. A client that pipelines two USER and PASS pairs on one connection is not admitted twice: the listener reads one command at a time, so the second pair meets a session that has already signed in and is refused. A release names the session that opened the maildrop and not the account, so an ending that arrives after the next session has already opened one cannot take it away from the client holding it. A hold nothing has touched for thirty minutes is also released, which is what answers if the ending is never registered at all; a client sitting on an open maildrop sends NOOP to keep it, and that counts. Deletions apply only at QUIT, which means an interrupted session deletes nothing and offers the same mail again on the next collection, while a QUIT still removes everything it marked. Holds live in memory and write nothing to the data volume, so a restart releases every one of them and there is no lock file to clear by hand. The operator guide covers what to tell an account holder whose client reports the mailbox in use.

items.title: An account can write as an address it holds, in the browser and over JMAP
items.body: A shared departmental address pointed at somebody's mailbox is an address they can send as, not only one they receive at. The compose form offers the choice only where there is one, so a mailbox owner with a single address sees the form they always saw, and JMAP returns one sending identity per permitted address so a client can present the same choice. The set is the account's own address plus every active alias pointed straight at it, with a subaddress folding to the address it extends and a catch-all never counting, since a catch-all claims every name in the domain. It follows one alias row rather than a chain, so an address that reaches the mailbox by way of a second alias is delivered there and is still not one the account may write. The picker is presentation only: the server recomputes the set on every send and writes the address from that set rather than the one the request carried, so nothing a form submitted reaches the header. The return path stays the account's own address, so a bounce comes back to the mailbox that sent the message rather than to the name it was sent under. A desktop client on the submission port derives the envelope from its configured identity and puts the alias in both places, and that is accepted: the envelope is resolved against the same set on every message, so an alias the account holds may be written there as well as in the header, and a subaddress folds to the address it extends.

items.title: A browser interface for mailbox owners and for you
items.body:
Read, search, compose, reply, reply to all, forward, move, flag, mark read, trash and purge, rendered on the server with client JavaScript as opt-in islands rather than a required runtime. Creating, renaming and deleting a folder is not offered, on any protocol. Remote and active content in a message is treated as hostile: images are held back until the reader asks for them, and asking reveals them for that message alone. The sign-in form takes fifty posts from one source address in five minutes and refuses that address for the rest of the window.

The administration surface covers domains, accounts, aliases, DKIM selectors, sign-in lockouts, the outbound queue and the audit log. It is held to the machine and browser the session was opened on: a request whose client address, browser or accepted language does not match the session is asked for the password again. The session row is kept, so the account carries on reading its mail and a failed attempt does not end the session. A mailbox session is not held that way: a phone moving between wifi and a cell network changes address, and mail stays open across the change.

items.title: The operator role is given to an existing account and taken back, from the console
items.body:
`blamepost init` creates an account carrying the operator role, and the account page in the administration interface is where an account that already exists is given it and where it is taken away again. Both of those controls ask for a reason before anything changes and both write a row: `blamepost audit read --action account.role_granted` and `--action account.role_revoked`. The create form on the same page carries a checkbox that gives a new account the role as it is made. That one asks for no reason and writes no grant row, so it reaches the trail as `account.created` with the role recorded on it, and an operator asking who was ever handed the console reads that action alongside the other two. The two row controls are not mirror images. A grant is offered and accepted only on an account that is in service, while the control that takes the role back sits on any row holding it whatever that row's status says, which the entry on granting the role sets out along with why.

Taking the role back is the narrow answer to an administrator whose credential has been taken, and to one who has moved on. It reaches a session that account already has open rather than waiting for the session to expire, because every request reads the role off the account row rather than off the session record. It leaves the mailbox signing in, sending and receiving, so answering a stolen password does not stop mail for a person whose mailbox was not the problem. The console will not let the last one go: taking the role from an account, suspending it, archiving it and disabling the domain its address belongs to are each measured against who would still be able to sign in afterwards, and each is refused when the answer is nobody. The refusal is recorded, at `blamepost audit read --action blamepost.web.last_administrator_removal_not_permitted`, and the way past it is to give the role to somebody else first.

A grant is the widest thing this server hands out, so the page says what it hands over: every mailbox owner's address, every hosted domain, the outbound spool, the signing keys and this audit trail, along with archiving an account and stopping a domain taking mail. It hands over nobody's messages. There is no command line verb for either direction; `init` grants the role while creating an account rather than on one that already exists, and the operator guide says so where it says how to recover a console nobody can sign in to.

items.title: An operator command line that answers questions
items.body: serve, init, account, domain, dkim, zone, credential, reports, dmarc, queue, doctor, audit, backup, restore and blobs. There is no alias verb among them: an address that forwards into a mailbox is added and withdrawn on the administration interface's aliases page. `account list` answers with the mailboxes that are still in the picture, which is the active ones, the suspended ones and any part way through an erasure, because the question an operator usually has is which mailboxes are live; `--include-archived` adds the archived rows, and that is where the address `account resume` takes back is found. doctor resolves your live DNS posture and names precisely which record is wrong rather than reporting a general failure. queue shows what is waiting, why, and what the far side actually said; `queue show <id>` narrows that to one message, every attempt made on it and how it ends if nothing changes. audit verifies the audit chain has not been truncated or rolled back and exports a range for an auditor. backup takes a verified encrypted backup and restore puts one back, with a rollback path if the restore itself fails. blobs compares the stored message bodies against the rows that reference them, and with verification turned on it unseals and re-hashes every one, so a body altered or truncated under a file nobody rewrites is found by you rather than by the account holder who opens the message. Almost every verb that destroys takes a recorded reason, and the ones that destroy in bulk take `--confirm` on top of it: reclaiming the bodies nothing references, purging the audit trail or a backup set, releasing a preservation order, and putting a restore or a rollback in place. Erasing an account and removing a domain name the destruction instead, with `--destroy` beside the reason: `account remove` without it archives the mailbox and keeps its mail, and `domain disable` is what stops mail for a domain without losing anything. Two verbs take no reason at all, and both destroy sealed signing keys: `blamepost dkim retire` and `blamepost dkim sweep`, because the row each writes carries what the signer said about the run rather than a sentence collected at the terminal. Nothing reclaims a body until it has been on disk for a day, because inside that window a body nothing references and a body whose row is still being written look alike. One process writes the data volume at a time. A command that has to write refuses while the server holds it and names the process that does, rather than decrypting a second copy and writing that back over whatever the server has recorded since. Stop the server for those. These reads are the exception and answer either way, off a read-only open: `account list` and `account show`, `domain list` and `domain show`, `dkim list` and `dkim records`, `zone preview` and `zone verify`, `credential list`, `credential show` and `credential bounces`, `reports list` and `reports show`, `blobs report`, `audit verify-chain` and `doctor`, which is exactly what you reach for while the server is up and behaving oddly. The refusal a write verb meets names that whole list, so you do not have to have read this to find it. The two zone reads are there because what they answer about is the zone at your DNS provider rather than anything on the volume. The entry on `blobs report` and `audit verify-chain` sets out what a read-only answer is bounded by. A read that is itself recorded is not among them: `audit read`, `account sieve` and `account messages` each take a reason and write the row saying somebody looked, so each needs the server stopped as a write does. The commands that read the outbound spool or a backup directory rather than the database are unaffected in either direction.

items.title: Outbound delivery, on one policy chain
items.body: Every outbound path composes the same chain rather than each growing its own: the receiver is resolved, MTA-STS is enforced against what its policy says, what the far side answered decides whether the message waits or stops, and a message that stops permanently produces a delivery report to the account that sent it. The budget is thirty five attempts, with waits of one minute, five, fifteen, an hour, and then four hours between every attempt after that, so a message is held for a little over five days before it is given up on and its sender told. That is the give-up time RFC 5321 section 4.5.4.1 asks for, and it is the scale a receiver schedules its own maintenance against: a peer down for an afternoon gets its mail delivered on the other side of the outage rather than bounced. `BLAMEPOST_OUTBOUND_RETRY` changes it, and `maxAttempts` is the half to move, since past the fifth attempt each one adds four hours. A message that instead runs out of that budget against a fault no receiver ever owned, such as a policy record that never settled or an envelope the composer would not take, ends the same way and reports under `4.4.7`. A receiver whose name never resolved spends the same budget and reports `4.4.4`. Both are transient rather than permanent on purpose: no peer was ever reached, so nothing has been established about the address at all, and a sender reading either one knows the message is worth sending again where a permanent code would tell them it is not. The class is transient while the report's own action is `failed`, which is the pairing RFC 3464 §2.3.3 and §2.3.4 describe for a queue entry that expired. Nothing is discarded because a failure was not recognized. Whether a message keeps its place or ends is read from the outcome the chain returns, never from the words a peer chose, so a receiver cannot talk this server into abandoning mail by phrasing a refusal to look like something else. Reports are rate limited per sender and in total, twenty five an hour to any one sender and five hundred an hour altogether, because a report is addressed to whoever the failed message claimed to be from, and on a forged run that is somebody who never wrote to you. A third ceiling holds the table those per-sender counters live in to four thousand and ninety six senders at once, and past it a sender not already being tracked is refused a report as well. That one is spent by variety rather than by volume, so a backscatter flood or a server hosting many domains can reach it and leave a legitimate sender with no bounce at all, which is the one failure shape indistinguishable from delivery. All three are counted per process and a restart clears them, and `blamepost audit read --action blamepost.mail.delivery.report_unsent` names everyone who was owed a report and did not get one. DANE is composed and only enforced when you tell the server your resolver validates DNSSEC, since a server cannot discover that about its own resolver and asserting it falsely is worse than not running DANE at all. REQUIRETLS goes on the wire when you ask for it, and a peer that does not advertise the extension is withheld from rather than delivered to.

items.title: The delivery reports this server receives about its own mail are read
items.body: A bounce for an account's message goes to that account, where a person reads it. Mail this server sends on its own behalf has nowhere to bounce that anybody checks: the TLS-RPT reports it owes the peers it delivers to go out from the postmaster address, and a report about one of them is the only signal that a reporting endpoint or an operator address has broken. The delivery reports it raises for accounts are not in that set, because RFC 5321 gives every such report an empty return path so one cannot start a run of reports about reports. What arrives for the postmaster is read and recorded, counted by the action each report states, and carried in the status the delivery layer reports about itself. No page or command renders those counts yet. Point BLAMEPOST_POSTMASTER at a real mailbox on a domain you host: the shipped default is built from the MX hostname, which is usually not a hosted domain, so a report addressed there is refused at the recipient and never arrives at all, and nothing else will tell you it is wrong. Nothing acts on a report, deliberately. Anyone can compose a well-formed report and send it to a postmaster address claiming any message failed, and acting on one would mean trusting a document a stranger wrote about mail you sent. There is nothing here that could prove the link either: no envelope identifier goes out, and a message a peer accepted and bounced afterwards left the outbound queue when it was accepted, so exactly the messages a report describes are the ones with no record left to match against. A report that cannot be read is recorded as unreadable rather than guessed at, with the reason kept, and ordinary mail to the postmaster is not counted as a failed report.

items.title: A message keeps the bytes it arrived with
items.body: Mail is not required to be valid UTF-8. RFC 6152 permits 8-bit content and legacy senders still produce it. A message carrying such bytes is stored and relayed exactly as it arrived, and the size reported for it, including the size a Sieve script tests against, is counted in octets rather than in characters. The two places that could quietly alter such a message both work in octets. The signature covers the bytes the sender wrote rather than a decoded copy, so what a receiver verifies is what left; hashing a decoded copy emits a signature that fails at every receiver, and returning one emits a signature over a message the sender never wrote. And it reads back byte for byte on every protocol: POP3 RETR and TOP, IMAP FETCH BODY[], and a partial fetch all return the stored octets, with the window a partial fetch takes measured in octets, which is what RFC 9051 section 6.4.5 counts in. What does leave a message unsigned has nothing to do with its character set: a domain this server holds no active selector for cannot be signed for, and that is recorded under an action of its own.

items.title: One stored copy of a shared message, and a delivery rewrites one that has gone short
items.body:
A message delivered to several accounts is stored once, named by the digest of its own content and sealed under the volume's key, so a mailing list message costs one copy on the volume rather than one per recipient. The account that arrives second files its row and reads the file already there.

That is also the one place a damaged body would spread. A file cut short by a restore that copied a prefix, by a write that stopped part way, or by a device that returned less than it was given is still a file at the right path, and every account handed the same message afterwards would inherit it and never have held a readable copy of its own. So a delivery compares the length of what is on disk against the message it is holding, and writes the message when the file is shorter than the sealed form of that message can be. It is the write that was about to happen anyway, and it lands atomically, so a repair cannot turn a short body into no body at all. Each one is recorded in the audit trail with the digest of the body it rewrote: a single repair is a bad sector, and a run of them is a volume to replace.

The length it compares against is a floor rather than an exact size, so read what it does not cover as carefully as what it does. It catches a large message cut below roughly three quarters of its length, a small one only when it is cut to a small fraction of it, and a body that changed without changing length not at all. Deciding any of those on every delivery would mean unsealing and re-hashing every message the volume already holds. Nothing is served for them either. IMAP and POP3 read the file, so they hash the stored octets back before returning them and refuse a body that does not hash to the digest naming it; the browser interface and JMAP render from the sealed row and never open the file at all. `blamepost blobs report --verify` names every file affected, and a body that will not open at all is refused in the same terms rather than reaching a client as a failure worth retrying.

items.title: The outbound queue has a bottom, and reaching it refuses mail rather than losing it
items.body: The queue shares one volume with the mailboxes, the message bodies and the audit trail, so it cannot be allowed to grow without a bound. Past its ceiling a submission is answered with a temporary code and the message stays in the sender's outbox, and an arriving message is answered the same way and stays with the peer that sent it, which is the party that can still do something about it. Mail arriving for forwarding stops short of the ceiling, at four fifths of it, so a flood aimed at an alias cannot spend the room your own accounts need in order to send. The delivery reports this server raises for senders stop at a tenth of it, which is the tightest of the three, so a queue that is filling does not also fill with notices about mail that already failed. Both a message count and a byte total apply, whichever is reached first, because depth is what every sweep pays and bytes are what the volume pays. queue flush claims each entry before attempting it, so two runs over one queue cannot attempt a message twice or move one out from under an attempt already in flight.

items.title: The health probes report whether mail is still moving
items.body: A queue that is filling and not draining reads from outside exactly like a healthy server: the ports are held, the store is open, the certificate is fresh, and mail is not leaving. Both probes carry a queue check, so a monitoring system finds that rather than the account holder whose message never arrived. It reduces the verdict from ok to degraded on three readings, and over the loopback interface it names which one fired; from anywhere else the answer is the verdict word alone. queue depth, or queue bytes, means the queue has filled past the point where it stops accepting mail for forwarding, which is not a warning level chosen for the probe but the reservation the queue already applies: reaching it means mail through an alias is being refused already and your own account holders are next. queue drain means mail is waiting and the sweep that retries it is not running. outbound transport means this build cannot put a message on the wire at all. Over the loopback interface the answer also carries how much is waiting, the depth at which forwarding stops, and how many messages the queue has refused since the server started. Neither probe refuses on any of them, so alert on degraded: a restart re-reads the same queue off the same volume and changes nothing about it, and withdrawing the interface takes away the console you would cancel the stuck mail from without moving any of the traffic that fills the queue. A queue that is stuck but small stays clean, deliberately, because a handful of messages retrying against one dead receiver is what an ordinary working server looks like; the operator guide says what to reach for instead when the question is about one destination rather than the whole queue.

items.title: TLS-RPT reports to the peers you deliver to
items.body: This server records how each delivery attempt's transport security went, for every domain it delivers to, and once a day it asks each of those domains where reports should go and submits an RFC 8460 aggregate report to the ones that answer. A domain that publishes no endpoint is sent nothing, and what that run judged for it is dropped rather than held. What is recorded is the successes and the failures that are genuinely about transport security; a refusal that has nothing to do with TLS, a full mailbox among them, is not recorded at all rather than counted as a broken handshake. Reports go where that domain's zone says at the moment of the run, and a destination the zone gives as a web address is posted to directly rather than composed as mail. One carries this server's hostname, the postmaster address as the contact a receiver replies to, the period it covers, the policy, the mail exchangers tried and the counts. No account address, no recipient, no subject and no message content is in one. blamepost does not yet read reports sent to your own endpoint; the operator guide says so plainly rather than leaving you publishing a record for nothing.

items.title: One container, one volume, no runtime dependencies
items.body: A two-stage build that runs as an unprivileged user, declares one data volume at /var/lib/blamepost, and is run by the compose file with every Linux capability dropped and no new privileges. NET_BIND_SERVICE is dropped with the rest, and 25, 143, 465, 587 and 4190 are still bound directly, because the compose file sets `net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start` to 0. That setting is namespaced to the container and changes nothing on the host. Host networking is the case it cannot serve, since the namespace is then the host's own: move each listener to a port above 1024 there and publish the standard one to it, and read what the operator guide says about the cost first, because a published port presents the mapping's address rather than the sender's, and that address is the one the per-peer connection and failure budgets are counted against. Nothing the image is configured to run goes through a shell. The application resolves nothing from a package registry at run time or at image build time, because the framework it composes is vendored in the tree and ships inside the tarball. The compose file runs the same image and keeps optional content scanning and a TLS terminator behind profiles that are off unless you ask for them.

items.title: A renewed certificate reaches the running server without a restart
items.body: blamepost issues no certificate: BLAMEPOST_TLS_CERT and BLAMEPOST_TLS_KEY name two files your certificate client writes, and every sixty to ninety days it rewrites both of them underneath a server that is already running. Both files are watched. SMTP on 25, submission on 465 and 587, IMAP on 143, POP3 on 110 and ManageSieve on 4190 read the certificate as each connection arrives, so the first connection after the watcher picks the change up, which is within half a minute of the rewrite, is answered with the new one. Webmail, the administration surface and JMAP on 8443 pick it up as well: that port builds its own TLS context out of the two files, so it is handed the renewed pair when the reload happens rather than re-reading it per connection, and the next browser to connect gets the new certificate with the port never rebound and open connections never dropped. No port is left behind and no restart is part of a renewal. Each reload writes a line naming the certificate path it rebuilt from, whether it was the certificate or the key that changed, and any port still holding the old certificate. That last list is empty on this build, because every port named above takes the renewal. A renewal caught half written, with the certificate replaced and the key not yet, is discarded rather than installed, and the server keeps serving the pair it already had until a complete one appears.

items.title: A completed restore says what it has not opened
items.body: `blamepost restore apply` verifies the bundle's signature, puts the volume in place, opens it and walks its audit chain. None of that opens a message body. A backup preserves whatever state the volume was in when it was taken, so mail that was already unreadable comes back unreadable, and a backup taken while mail was arriving can carry a row whose body had not been written yet. The verb closes by sending you to `blamepost blobs report --verify`, which unseals every body a row names and hashes it back against that row, and then to `blamepost doctor` for the DKIM state a restore rewinds. Both are worth running before the server starts, and both answer while it holds the volume as well, from a read-only open whose rows stop at the last write to disk; each says how old that reading is before it reports anything. `doctor` counts bodies without opening one, so `blobs report --verify` is the only thing here that reads a message body at all. A restore onto a host with no data directory to move aside says so rather than naming a directory it kept.

items.title: Preservation orders are placed, read back and lifted from the command line
items.body: A court's order to keep records is answered with `blamepost account hold`, and every hard delete refuses those messages afterwards on IMAP, POP3, JMAP and webmail alike, an account erasure included. Finding the records comes first, so `blamepost account messages` lists what an account holds with the id each message is named by, the date it arrived here, the date the message shows, the sender and the subject, and marks anything already under an order; it never prints a body, and reading somebody's mail list takes a recorded reason the way reading their filter scripts does. `blamepost account holds` reads the orders back with the matter each cites, the custodian answerable for the records and who placed it, which is how you establish that an order is in force rather than trusting the command that placed it. An order names messages rather than a mailbox, so mail arriving afterwards is not swept into it silently, and it carries no expiry date, because nothing here sweeps one and a date recorded against an order would read as an end this server never acts on. `blamepost account release` lifts one and takes `--confirm` and an `--approver`, because the next expunge, POP3 commit, JMAP destroy or erasure on those messages will destroy them and an order is not lifted by whoever happens to be at the keyboard. Naming a message the account does not hold is refused by name and exits non-zero rather than reporting a duty that was never taken on. Placing and lifting each write a hash-chained row that `blamepost audit read` returns.

items.title: The installed package carries the documents it sends you to
items.body: `npm install @blamejs/blamepost` puts ROADMAP.md, THREAT-MODEL.md, ARCHITECTURE.md and LTS-CALENDAR.md on disk beside the README, along with the contributing, governance, support and conduct documents, so a link followed out of any page in the tarball resolves against a file that is there. Packing refuses a tarball in which any shipped document links to a file the tarball does not contain, so the set stays closed as documents are added.

items.title: `doctor` holds the sealed signing keys against the records that name them
items.body: `blamepost doctor` prints a `signing keys` line that reads the data directory's `keys` folder and the DKIM selector records together. It names the sealed private keys on the volume that no record claims, five of them by name and a count of any beyond that, which is signing material nothing on this server will use or remove and which every backup taken from then on carries, and it names every active selector whose key is not on the volume, which is a domain whose mail is leaving unsigned right now. A retiring selector with no key is neither and is not counted: retirement destroys the private half and keeps the record published through the overlap. Run while the server holds the volume, the records stop at its last write to disk while the keys folder is live, so a key written after that moment is counted apart as one the records had not reached rather than named as one nothing claims: an operator is never sent to destroy signing material their server is using.

items.title: `domain remove` reports the signing material it destroyed
items.body:
Withdrawing a domain prints the number of DKIM selector records and the number of sealed private keys it erased, and reminds you to pull the records from the zone yourself, because nothing here removes a DNS record on any setting. `store.domains.remove` returns `keysErased` and `keysAlreadyGone` beside `selectorsRemoved`, and `store.domains.removeSelector` returns `keyErased`, so a caller can tell a key this call destroyed from one a retirement had already destroyed.

One outcome leaves you work, and it is printed rather than only counted. A sealed key that could not be destroyed after its records had already gone is named in the output, under the file name it is now sitting at, and comes back as `keysLeftAside`. Nothing on this server can find it again, because the record that named it is what is gone, so no second run of the command reaches it and the audit row for the withdrawal records a failure. Delete the file by hand: whoever holds one signs mail as that domain for as long as the volume and its backups last, including after somebody else takes the name on.

items.title: `UID SEARCH` answers in unique identifiers
items.body: IMAP clients may search with either spelling of the command. `SEARCH` answers in message sequence numbers and `UID SEARCH` answers in unique identifiers, as RFC 9051 §6.4.9 requires, and both are served by the same handler over the same keys, so a key one form refuses is refused by the other. One shape does not cross: a search term sent as an IMAP literal reaches the sequence-number spelling and not the identifier one, which answers `BAD` where the term should be. The search keys keep the meaning §6.4.4 gives them under both, so a bare sequence set is still a sequence set and a `UID` key is still identifiers. Apart from that one shape, only the answer changes. A client that keeps a cache between sessions asks for the identifier form because a sequence number means nothing outside the session that issued it, so this is the form that lets a mailbox be reopened without re-reading it.

items.title: `doctor` holds the spooled message bodies against the descriptors that name them
items.body: A message waiting for a retry is two files: the message itself, and the descriptor carrying the recipient, the attempt count and what the far side said. The ordinary listing reads descriptors, so a body whose descriptor is not there appears nowhere in it, while the queue's own ceiling is measured off the volume and weighs that body regardless: the room is spent with nothing in the ordinary listing to explain where it went. So both `blamepost queue list` and `blamepost doctor` account for those bodies separately, the first naming every one of them and the second naming five with a count of any beyond that, and `blamepost queue remove <id> --reason ...` acts on the id either one prints. A body written in the last five minutes is left out, because the pair is legitimately half on disk between the two writes and a message arriving normally must not be reported as one to delete.

items.title: `blobs report` and `audit verify-chain` answer while the server is running
items.body:
The two verbs you most want during an incident answer without the mail server being stopped first, from a read-only open of the same volume: the encrypted database is decrypted into a working copy that is never written back, the sealed database key is never re-sealed, no audit checkpoint is anchored, and the database handle refuses a write wherever one is issued. `account list`, `account show`, `domain list`, `domain show`, `dkim list`, `dkim records`, `zone preview`, `zone verify`, `reports list`, `reports show` and `doctor` take the same path, and the refusal a write verb meets while the server holds the volume names all of them. Each prints how old the answer is before printing the answer, measured from the moment the server last wrote the volume to disk, and under `--json` that arrives inside an envelope so a script stops parsing rather than believing a stale answer.

`audit verify-chain` reaches the same verdict it reaches against a stopped server, signatures included. It walks the chain's own row hashes, verifies every checkpoint signature, and holds the record beside the volume against the rows, which is the combination a rewritten trail cannot satisfy: recomputing the hashes is cheap and forging a signature is not. What it covers is the chain up to the server's last write to disk, and the chain only ever grows, so that is a verified prefix rather than a partial reading.

`blobs report` reads two things that move at different speeds, and says so rather than guessing. The rows stop at the last write to disk while the blob directory is live, so a message delivered in between has its body on the volume and its row still in the server's own copy. That body is reported as one the rows had not reached, is not counted against the verdict, and is not reclaimable by anything. Everything else in the report is unaffected by how old the rows are: a row naming a body that is not on disk is missing whenever it is read, and `--verify`, which unseals every referenced body and hashes it back against the digest naming it, finds an altered body whenever it is read. `blamepost doctor` runs the same reader, so both reach a verdict on the message bodies and on the signing keys rather than reporting those two checks as not done.

items.title: `queue show` says what each attempt met, and how the message ends if nothing changes
items.body:
`blamepost queue show <id>` prints one queued message on its own: the recipient, the sender, when it was queued, its size, and then every attempt made on it, oldest first, with the host each attempt reached and what that receiver said in its own words. A listing carries one row per message and the last reason only, so two attempts refused for different reasons read there as a single refusal. Telling them apart is what separates a fault that moved from a fault that persists, and it is the question asked first when an account holder is waiting on a message.

The closing lines say where the message is headed: how much of its retry budget is spent, when the next attempt falls due, and who is told if the budget runs out. A message whose sender is the empty reverse path is itself a delivery report, so there is nobody to tell, and the line says so rather than naming an address that would not be written.

Take the id from `blamepost queue list`. An id this server did not mint is refused rather than turned into a path, and a well formed id with nothing behind it reports that the message is no longer waiting, which covers delivery, a message given up on, and a cancellation alike. `blamepost audit read --action blamepost.mail.queue.message_removed` says whether an operator removed it.

items.title: Mail between two accounts on this server is filed locally
items.body:
A message addressed to an account this server hosts is written into that account's mailbox, whether a mail client on 587 or 465 sent it, the compose form in the browser sent it, or a JMAP client called `EmailSubmission/set`. It does not depend on the MX record resolving, on the machine reaching its own public address, or on the MTA-STS and DANE policy the domain publishes about itself, and it takes no room in the outbound queue.

The local copy gets the delivery an arriving message gets: the recipient's Sieve script runs, the quota and the retention floor apply, and the filed copy carries the DKIM signatures the message was signed with. Aliases resolve first, so an address that forwards to a mailbox here is filed there and one that forwards off this server leaves over the outbound path. An envelope naming recipients here and elsewhere is split, and only the ones that leave count against the queue. An address this server hosts and cannot deliver to, such as a suspended mailbox, is reported to the sender rather than sent onward.

`docs/operator-guide.md` covers this under Mail between two mailboxes on this server.

items.title: A hosted-DNS credential, and the two commands that read your zone with it
items.body:
Left alone, this server publishes no DNS record: it prints what to publish and you put it in the zone. What `BLAMEPOST_ZONE_PROVIDER` adds is reading, and one write from the console that the next entry covers. Name a provider, seal a token onto the volume, and `blamepost zone preview <domain>` holds your zone up against the DKIM selector records this server expects to find in it, while `blamepost zone verify <domain>` reads each of those twice, from the provider and through a resolver, and separates a record that has not propagated yet from one that resolves to something else. The second of those is the one that matters: a resolver answering with a value this server did not publish means mail is being judged against it, and no amount of waiting fixes that.

The setting names no provider by default, and that default is the whole of the posture. With it at `none` no credential is opened, no provider client is built and this process sends nothing to a DNS provider at all. The other four settings in the group are refused while it stands, because a sealed credential and an `MX` switch that reach nothing look exactly like a zone writer that is running. A `BLAMEPOST_ZONE_ENDPOINT` written as a literal cloud metadata address stops the start, and so does a literal private, loopback or link-local address unless `BLAMEPOST_ZONE_ALLOW_INTERNAL_ENDPOINT` is set.

Size the grant against the write set rather than against the two read commands, because the console publishes a `_dmarc` record through the same credential.
