The set is fixed: the sender policy and DMARC records, the DKIM selector records, the MTA-STS identifier and host, the TLS reporting address, and DANE associations under `_tcp`, each at one address under one hosted domain. A type outside that list, an address outside it, a wildcard, and any name in another zone are refused before a request leaves. The `MX` record sits behind `BLAMEPOST_ZONE_ALLOW_MX_WRITES`, which is off: repointing `MX` moves delivery away from this server, so it is the one change this server could not report on afterwards.

The token is a credential and it is sealed before it reaches disk. `blamepost zone token set --token-file <path> --reason <text>` reads it from a file rather than from a command line, which is in the shell history and in the process list, refuses a file holding anything a bearer token cannot carry, seals it with the vault passphrase bound to the zone writer, and writes it to `keys/zone-token.sealed` beside the sealed DKIM private keys. A value the vault sealed for anything else, a DKIM key copied over that file among them, is refused rather than sent to the provider. A raw token in the configuration is refused at start rather than used, because opening a seal passes an unsealed value straight through and one written in the clear would authenticate exactly as well while being readable to anyone who can read the file. A deployment that injects secrets can supply the sealed value as `BLAMEPOST_ZONE_API_TOKEN` instead; supplying both stops the start rather than one quietly winning. `blamepost zone token clear --reason <text> --confirm` erases it from the volume, and erasing it revokes nothing: every backup bundle taken while it was there carries it, so revoke at the provider as well. Both credential verbs write the volume and need the server stopped; both reads answer while it runs.

Every verb here takes a reason and leaves an audit row, refusals included. There is no `apply` verb on the command line: performing a change set needs the data volume and a running server holds it, so an apply here would mean stopping the mail server to edit a TXT record. `docs/operator-guide.md` covers this under Letting this server write its own DNS records.

items.title: What receivers report about your domains, read from the command line
items.body:
`blamepost reports list` is the reading a DMARC policy is moved on, one block per hosted domain over the last thirty days or over a range you name with `--from` and `--to`: the volume receivers counted, how much of it aligned on either identifier, the sending addresses that failed on both with the largest first, and which organizations reported and when their most recent report arrived. A hosted domain nothing has reported on prints a line saying so rather than a row of zeroes, because a domain nobody reports on and a domain nobody spoofs otherwise read the same.

A report counts toward that arithmetic only where this server authenticated the message that carried it. Anybody who can send mail to the address your `rua=` record publishes can compose a well formed report, so the counting is over the reports whose carrier passed DMARC for the organization the report names as its author. The volume that condition leaves out is printed beside every total rather than dropped, and `--include-unauthenticated` recomputes every total over the wider set, the failing sources included, for when you are working out why a number looks wrong.

`blamepost reports show <id>` opens one aggregate report: the policy the reporter judged your mail against, the organization that sent it and their contact mailbox, what this server concluded about the message that carried it, and the sending addresses it counted with their dispositions and alignment results. Ids come from the listing, and `--limit` sets how many rows each list prints, with what is not printed counted rather than dropped. Both verbs write nothing and answer while the server is running.

`blamepost reports forget <address> --reason <text> --confirm` answers an erasure request from somebody who has no account here. It destroys every stored report row naming that address together with the key each row was sealed under, so what is left in the write-ahead log reads as absent rather than as ciphertext, and it prints how many rows named the address beside how many were destroyed, so a row that matched and stayed cannot read as one that went. It writes the volume and needs the server stopped. The confirmation is required because the address on the line does not show what the verb reaches: it is matched against the envelope sender and the recipients of a forensic report and against the contact mailbox a reporting organization writes into its own aggregate reports, so an address belonging to a reporter takes that reporter's counting with it.

Forensic reports are not listed or shown. Those rows hold the envelope of somebody with no account here, and the erasure verb is the only thing on the command line that reaches them. Nothing here publishes a DNS record or moves a policy, and reports sent to your own TLS-RPT endpoint are still not read. `docs/operator-guide.md` covers all of it under What peers report about your domains.

items.title: Whether a domain's reports carry the next DMARC policy step
items.body:
`blamepost dmarc status <domain>` answers whether a hosted domain's reports carry the move from `p=none` to `p=quarantine`, and from there to `p=reject`. It prints the policy the domain publishes today, which step is next, every rule that step is measured against with what the rule asks for beside what the domain has, and the `_dmarc` record text for all three levels whichever way the answer goes. The thresholds are constants rather than settings and the command prints the ones in force, so there is no gate to lower and nothing to read out of a document. It exits zero either way, because a domain a fortnight into collecting reports is the ordinary state of a domain on its way to `p=quarantine` rather than a fault.

The counting behind it is over the reports whose carrier this server authenticated and over nothing else, and no flag on this verb changes that. Anybody who can send mail to the address a `rua=` record publishes can compose a well formed report, so a step taken on the wider reading is a step taken by whoever wanted it taken.

A sending address failing both alignments over the floor holds the step until somebody writes down what it is. `blamepost dmarc mark <domain> --source <address> --disposition <what> --reason <text>` is where that goes: `not-ours` for an address that is not yours, whose failures are what a policy exists to stop, and `ours-and-fixed` for a sending path of yours whose alignment has been corrected. The reporters get to contradict the second one: an address marked fixed that keeps failing in a window ending well after the marking was written blocks the step again. The marking is an audit row carrying who wrote it, when, and your sentence in its own column, and a later marking for the same address supersedes it while both stay readable. The address is not written into the row, because it belongs to somebody with no account here: what identifies the source is the keyed digest the report rows are already indexed by, and `blamepost reports forget` is the erasure path for the copy that already exists. `blamepost dmarc markings <domain>` reads back what is in force, and a trail it could not read is reported as that rather than as a domain nobody has marked anything for.

Stepping down is not gated. There is no evidence to gather and no threshold to clear: mail being discarded is answered by publishing the weaker record and looking afterwards. Every reading prints the weaker record beside the verdict, and `blamepost dmarc preview <domain>` prints the record text on its own over no data volume at all, so it answers while the server runs, after it has stopped, and on a machine whose database will not open. A `pct` tag is never carried into a printed record, since RFC 7489 section 6.3 makes an absent one mean the whole of the mail and RFC 9989 removed the tag. A `rua` tag is added when the published record carries none, pointing at the address `BLAMEPOST_POSTMASTER` names: point that setting at a mailbox on a domain you host, because its default is built from the MX hostname and reports sent there are refused at `RCPT`.

None of these commands publishes a record. `status` and `mark` write to the audit trail and need the server stopped, and `preview` reads DNS and nothing else. The DMARC page in the administration console is where a record is published, and the next entry covers it. `docs/operator-guide.md` covers this under Moving a domain's DMARC policy.

items.title: Publishing a DMARC record from the administration console
items.body:
The DMARC page in the console shows the `_dmarc` record each policy level would be published as, and where `BLAMEPOST_ZONE_PROVIDER` names a provider it publishes one. Pick a single domain, read where its policy stands and what each level would be, write down why you are changing it, and press Prepare. The server reads the zone at your provider and answers with the change set that would be performed, line by line: the record being written, and any extra record at `_dmarc.<domain>` that would be removed. Nothing is written by that read. Type the domain back and the set is performed.

The set that is performed is the one you read. It is held in the running server between the two pages rather than recomputed at the second, so a zone that moved in between stops the write with a refusal naming the drift instead of overwriting whatever is there now. A confirmation carrying a different held set than the page it came from is refused for the same reason, and a set already performed cannot be performed again. Change sets expire fifteen minutes after they are computed.

Removal reaches `_dmarc.<domain>` and nothing else. Two DMARC records at one name is a permanent error to every receiver that reads them, so publishing reduces that address to the one record rather than adding a second; an address the change set is silent about is not read and not touched. Any change set at all takes the typed confirmation, and one carrying more changes than the gate performs is refused before a request leaves.

After the write the record is read back twice, at the provider and through a resolver, and the page says which of three states it landed in: both agree, the provider holds it and no resolver has answered with it yet, or a resolver is answering with something else. The last one does not clear on its own and means mail is being judged against a record this server did not write.

Stepping up is offered only for the level the reporting evidence carries, which is the same rule `blamepost dmarc status` reports. Stepping down is offered whenever the record is readable, because mail being discarded is answered by publishing the weaker record and looking afterwards. Every prepare and every publish leaves an audit row naming the operator, the domain, what changed and the reason they wrote; a refusal answers `application/problem+json` under a type naming which rule refused. `docs/operator-guide.md` covers this under Publishing a DMARC record from the console.

items.title: Each account's JMAP capabilities name what the server will accept
items.body:
Every account in the session document at `/jmap/session` now carries the values a JMAP client reads before it draws anything. Under `urn:ietf:params:jmap:mail`: `maxMailboxesPerEmail` is `1`, `maxMailboxDepth` is `1`, `maxSizeMailboxName` is `128`, `maxSizeAttachmentsPerEmail` is `0`, `emailQuerySortOptions` is empty and `mayCreateTopLevelMailbox` is `false`. Under `urn:ietf:params:jmap:submission`: `maxDelayedSend` is `0` and `submissionExtensions` is empty.

Each value is the one the matching method already applies. A message is in one mailbox, mailboxes are flat and cannot be created over JMAP, a query sorts on nothing, and a file reaches a message through the compose form rather than through a blob upload. A client reading an empty capability object filled these in from its own defaults, which is how a Send Later field or a New Mailbox button reaches a mailbox owner over a server that does neither.

`EmailSubmission/set` now refuses a `sendAt` naming a time still to come, with `invalidProperties` naming that property. The message was previously sent at once and answered with a `sendAt` of the moment it went, so a client that scheduled mail for the morning had it delivered immediately and was told it was scheduled.

items.title: Paging a mailbox over JMAP
items.body:
`Email/query` reads `position` and `limit`, so a client can reach past the first page of a mailbox. It answers newest first over the newest 1000 messages of the mailbox `filter.inMailbox` names, a negative `position` counts back from the oldest message in that range, and a `limit` asks for up to 50 ids and is capped there, which is the ceiling `Email/get` takes in one call. The answer reports the `position` it started at and the `limit` it applied. A request reaching past the newest 1000 messages is refused `requestTooLarge`; IMAP pages a mailbox without that ceiling.

`total` is in the answer when the request sets `calculateTotal` to true, and is the count of the whole result rather than of the page. It was previously present on every answer and carried the number of ids in the page, so a mailbox of two hundred messages reported a total of fifty.

The filter conditions are `inMailbox`, `text`, `from`, `to` and `body`. A filter naming any other condition is refused `unsupportedFilter`, a `sort` naming a property is refused `unsupportedSort`, an `anchor` is refused `anchorNotFound`, and `collapseThreads` set to true is refused `invalidArguments`. Each of the four was previously read and dropped: a client asking for flagged mail was answered with every message in the mailbox, with nothing in the answer to say the condition went unread.

items.title: Opening a reply to an HTML message costs time in proportion to the body's length
items.body:
Reducing a message's markup to quotable text walks the body once, from a position that only moves forward, so the work is proportional to the body's length rather than to its square. The markup arrives from whoever sent the message, and a body can be a long run of opening angle brackets with no closing bracket after any of them. The cost of reading such a body lands on the account holder, on the request that opens the reply or forward, rather than on the sender.

The ceiling on how much of a message gets quoted does not stand in for that bound, because it is applied to the result: it decides how long the draft is rather than how much text was walked to produce it. A stored body reaches the message ceiling, which is 50 MiB unless you lower `maxMessageBytes`.

items.title: The security posture is the boot sequence, not a set of flags
items.body:
Cross-site request forgery protection, origin and fetch-metadata checks, the bot guard, cookie prefixes, Trusted Types and encrypted sessions are wired into the request lifecycle, over a store whose sensitive columns are sealed at rest. There is no configuration that turns any of them off. The server additionally refuses to start when the vault, the at-rest encryption, the audit signing posture, the clock check, the Node version floor, the transport minimum, the data directory permissions, the runtime environment or an operator-installed certificate authority in the runtime trust store is not what a production deployment requires, and it names the predicate that refused.

One of those needs a firewall rule rather than a setting. Opening the store sends one SNTP query over UDP port 123 to a public time server, and a second to a fallback if the first does not answer, then compares the answer against this machine's clock, because the audit trail's timestamps are what an auditor reads and a host that has drifted writes a trail that is wrong without looking wrong. An hour or more of drift refuses the boot and names the number. Five minutes or more writes a warning and the boot continues, and anything under that writes an ordinary line naming the drift. No answer at all writes a warning too, `ntp warning: NTP unreachable`, and the boot goes on with the clock unchecked. That line suggests BLAMEJS_NTP_STRICT=1, which is already the default and governs measured drift rather than an unanswered query, so the fix is to open UDP 123 outbound or to point BLAMEJS_NTP_SERVERS at a time source you run. BLAMEJS_SKIP_NTP_CHECK=1 drops the query and the warning with it. None of the three is a substitute for the host synchronizing its own clock; this runs once, at boot.

items.title: Post-quantum first, with classical algorithms beside rather than instead
items.body: Where the choice is this project's to make, the key encapsulation is an ML-KEM-1024 and P-384 hybrid, the audit checkpoints are signed with SLH-DSA-SHAKE-256f, digests and key derivation are SHA3-512 and SHAKE256, passwords are hashed with Argon2id, and everything sealed on the volume is encrypted with XChaCha20-Poly1305. Release artifacts carry an ML-DSA-65 sidecar signature from the first release cut after the signing key is set up, which the entry on verifying a release covers. Where an interoperable wire format settles the algorithm instead, it does not, and DKIM is the case worth knowing about. The DKIM-Signature a= tag draws from an IANA registry that has no post-quantum value, so outbound mail is signed with both an Ed25519 and an RSA selector and a receiver that has not implemented RFC 8463 still gets an authenticated message. Both of those are classical, and nothing post-quantum stands beside them until a key type is registered. The transport key exchange is a different shape: every listener names the set it accepts, leads it with post-quantum hybrids and asks a peer that implements one to use it, which the entry on those listeners covers. What relays unsigned rather than altered is a message the signer refused: a domain holding no active selector or only half a pair, a key file that cannot be read, one carrying no seal, and one the vault will not open. Each leaves a row carrying the code that says which.

items.title: A hosted domain signs with both DKIM algorithms or with neither, never with one
items.body: Ed25519 and RSA-SHA256 are the two algorithms a DKIM signature can name, and a hosted domain that signs at all publishes one selector of each. `blamepost domain add` and `blamepost init` mint the pair as they take the domain on; a domain added from the administration interface is hosted before it holds any key, and its mail leaves unsigned until you mint one there. There is no setting that turns one of them off and no verb an operator can reach withdraws half a pair: retiring names a pair and takes both halves, so a domain cannot be left signing with one algorithm. If a receiver mishandles the second signature header, publish both records anyway. RFC 6376 requires a verifier to ignore a signature whose algorithm it does not implement (section 3.3.4) and says it should keep checking the rest (section 6.1), and a receiver that cannot do that will also mishandle mail from any sender part way through a key rotation. A domain that does hold one algorithm, which a mint or a retirement interrupted part way can leave behind, signs nothing until it holds both again, and the refusal says which half is missing. The way back from either half is to retire what is left and mint a fresh pair, with the domain unsigned between those two steps. Retirement is named by the Ed25519 selector and looks for the RSA half under that name with `-rsa` on the end, which is how every pair is minted, so a domain left holding only its RSA half is retired by naming the Ed25519 selector that half was minted beside: the surviving name with `-rsa` taken off it. `blamepost dkim list` prints what is left, and a name that matches nothing is refused with the selectors the domain does hold.

items.title: This server does not relay for an address range, and says so at start rather than later
items.body: Granting relay to a range of source addresses stops the boot, naming the setting and what to do instead. The reason is worth knowing before you reach for it elsewhere: every mail listener here requires TLS before it will accept an envelope, so a device that gets as far as naming a recipient on port 25 has already completed a handshake, and a device that can do that can authenticate on the submission port. The only device an address range could have served that an account cannot is one with no encryption at all, and that device is answered `530 5.7.0 Must issue a STARTTLS command first` at `MAIL FROM`, before it has named a recipient. The range carried the whole risk of relaying for anything else on that network and bought nothing. Give the printer or the application server an account. A range names a segment rather than a party, so when one machine on it is compromised the only lever is withdrawing the range and taking the printer down with it, while an account is suspended on its own and has a mailbox where a delivery failure can be read.

items.title: The certificate is read before anything binds, and doctor reads it too
items.body: A certificate that has expired is a file that is still present and still readable, so a server that checked only for a file would start, take every port, and refuse every connection offered to it, while reporting itself healthy. The pair is opened before the first listener binds. A certificate whose validity has closed or has not opened yet, a key that belongs to a different certificate, a file that is not a certificate at all, a key the vault will not unseal, and either file the process cannot read each stop the start and name both paths and the reason. Two of those are what a first boot meets. This image drops privileges, so a key left readable only by root is a key it cannot read; and a certificate reported as not valid until a date ahead of now is usually a host whose clock is wrong rather than a certificate to reissue. `blamepost doctor` reports the same reading without starting anything: the expiry date and the days left, whether the key matches, whether the certificate covers the name this server announces, and whether the file holds the full chain or only the leaf. That last one is the mistake that survives testing, because a browser fetches a missing issuer itself and a sending mail server does not, so a leaf-only certificate passes a check in your browser and stops your mail. A certificate that is wrong but still usable is reported and logged and does not stop the server, because every peer that does not check the thing it got wrong is served exactly as before. The private key is opened only to compare it against the certificate, and never appears in a report or a log line.

items.title: The health probes read the certificate, so a renewal that stopped running is found before mail stops
items.body: A renewal client that dies is the slowest outage this server has. Nothing changes for weeks, and then every peer stops talking to it at once. Nothing else either probe reads moves while it happens: the listeners stay bound and the store stays open for the whole of it. So `/healthz` and `/readyz` carry a `certificate` check that reads the pair on disk on every poll rather than once at boot, since a reading taken at boot describes the certificate the renewal replaced. The verdict drops from `ok` to `degraded` as soon as the certificate is inside a fortnight of expiring, the chain is incomplete, the name this server announces is not covered, or the two files no longer agree. Over the loopback interface, which is where the container's own health check runs, the answer also carries the days remaining, a flag saying whether the pair is one this server could present at all, and the names of the readings that failed. Alert on `degraded`. The probe reduces its verdict and never refuses, including for a certificate that has already run out, and that is deliberate: refusing would take a server out of rotation while it is still carrying mail for every peer, withdraw the interface you would have read the reason from, and invite a restart that this server would refuse to complete, since it does not start on a certificate it cannot present. Renew the certificate and the running server picks it up on every port it binds, with no restart.

items.title: REQUIRETLS withholds a message from a peer that will not promise to encrypt it
items.body: `BLAMEPOST_REQUIRE_TLS` asks every outbound envelope for REQUIRETLS. RFC 8689 lets a sender tell a receiver to hold a message back rather than deliver it over a connection it could not encrypt, and with the setting on, the keyword goes on the `MAIL FROM` line of every peer whose EHLO advertises the extension. A peer that does not advertise it is not delivered to at all: the message is offered to each mail exchanger for the recipient's domain in turn, and permanently failed with `5.7.30` once none of them has advertised it. Section 4.1 requires that rather than a quiet fall back to sending in the clear, and it is the whole value of the setting, because a sender told the message went cannot otherwise tell an encrypted delivery from one the receiver never promised to encrypt. It is off by default for the same reason it is worth having: most receivers do not implement the extension, so a server that asks every peer for it stops delivering to most of them. Turn it on where you know your correspondents support it. A host that was skipped before the send, a DANE lookup failing mid-rollover, never answered the question, so a run containing one stays deferrable rather than bouncing. Transport security on the way out is enforced whatever this is set to: MTA-STS applies to every outbound message and refuses a peer whose certificate does not match its published policy, and DANE applies once you have told the server that its resolver validates DNSSEC. That last condition is not a formality and DANE does nothing without it: the standard forbids acting on a TLSA record that was not validated, and no server can discover that fact about the resolver it was pointed at. Know what neither of them reaches. Against a receiving domain that publishes no MTA-STS policy and no TLSA record, the mail exchanger this server connects to is named by a DNS answer nothing validated, and a host holding a valid certificate for a name of its own satisfies every check that is left. The connection is encrypted, and it may be encrypted to somebody else. What closes that is the receiving domain publishing one of the two, which is not yours to publish for them.

items.title: The cross-site gate stands down only for a caller with no ambient credential, and never stands the origin check down
items.body: A state change arriving at the browser surface is held to a double submit token and to an origin cross-check, and the one waiver either of them has is narrow and deliberate. It applies to a caller that sends no cookie at all, and to nothing else. Such a caller has no ambient credential for a page on another site to spend, which is the whole of what this class of attack is, and it carries no token back, so demanding one would be an outage on the JMAP bearer path rather than a defense. A request that sends a cookie is validated whatever else it carries. An authorization header buys nothing: a header is something the party composing the request writes, so its presence is evidence of nothing, and this server resolves a session from the cookie before it reads one anyway, which means a request carrying both is authenticated by exactly the credential the gate exists to protect. The origin cross-check is never waived, by that caller or any other. It answers a different question than the token compare does, and there is no reading of a request being cookieless under which a cross-origin state change becomes acceptable, so a bearer client asking for one from another site is refused like anybody else. What this means in practice: a token-only client works with no token to send, a browser session is checked on every state change, and neither one can be talked out of the origin check by anything it puts in a header.

items.title: A mailbox reused for a new account tells clients to forget what they cached
items.body: Every IMAP folder carries a number that tells a client whether the identifiers it remembers still mean the same messages, and the standard requires that number never to go backwards or repeat. Taken from the clock alone, deleting an account and creating the same address again within the same second would produce that number twice while the message identifiers underneath restarted from one, and a client holding a cache from before would keep it and map what it remembered onto whatever now holds those identifiers, which after a re-provisioning is somebody else's mail. So it comes from the clock only when that is higher than anything the volume has ever issued, so it climbs across a re-provisioning, across a restore from backup, and across a clock correction while the server runs, and it refuses rather than wrapping if it ever reaches the ceiling the format allows.

items.title: Correcting the server's clock costs no mail and hands back no spent budget
items.body: Several rules here are windows rather than states, and a window measured against the wall clock moves when an operator fixes the time or a time service steps it. Three of them would. A POP3 session holds its mailbox exclusively while it is open, and timed on the wall clock a correction forward past the timeout would hand the mailbox to somebody else while the first session still had it. That is worse than it sounds, because the protocol only applies deletions when a session ends cleanly, so the marks that session had made would go with it and the account holder would watch deleted mail come back. A correction backwards has the mirror problem: an abandoned session's lock could not expire until the clock caught up. The bound on how many delivery reports this server will send in an hour would reset on a step as well, handing back the whole allowance without any time having passed, which matters because that bound exists to stop a forged run turning this server into somebody else's flood. And a transport report could claim a period that ended before it began. So the first two measure elapsed time from a source an operator cannot move, and so do the three budgets behind a sign in: the one kept against a mailbox, the smaller one kept against a single machine, and the thirty days a machine stays familiar to a mailbox it has signed in from. A step in either direction ends none of those early or late. The third stays a wall-clock instant, because RFC 8460 puts it in front of a receiver as a real date and files the report under it, so a start later than the present is re-anchored to now rather than withheld: the counts underneath it are observations the receiver is owed, and letting a clock correction suppress them would be the same failure in other clothes. What deliberately uses the calendar is the outbound retry schedule, because a message waiting to be retried has to survive a restart and an elapsed count does not. Two budgets are still counted against the wall clock, and both are ceilings rather than mail: the authentication failures each listener counts against one source address over a quarter of an hour, and the five minute window in front of the browser sign in form. A correction forward can end either of those early.

items.title: A listener held back on purpose is not reported as one that failed
items.body: A listener has four states rather than two, and only one of them is a fault. It took its port, or the configuration did not turn it on, or it is enabled and deliberately held back with the server's own sentence saying why, or it was enabled and expected to bind and did not. Only the last is a failure. This matters most on the very first boot, which every operator passes through: port 25 holds itself back while no domain is hosted, because a server accepting mail for recipients it knows nothing about is collecting a stranger's mail. Reporting that as a port that failed to bind would make a fresh container read as unhealthy for the whole window between coming up and being configured, while submission, mailbox access and the browser interface were all bound and serving. Anything acting on that reading would treat the server as broken, and an orchestrator watching liveness would restart it in a loop, which fixes none of the causes and takes down the interface the operator was about to finish setup in. So liveness answers degraded rather than failing: the process is worth keeping and something is held back, said in one answer. Readiness is what refuses when a listener was expected to bind and did not, because stopping traffic is the response that fits; a listener held back on purpose reduces readiness to degraded rather than failing it, for the same reason liveness does. A store that will not open fails both, since that is the one condition a restart can address. The health probe writes its verdict, so a container runtime carries the reason beside the failing streak instead of an empty string, and the same distinction reaches the console: starting the server lists what bound and what is being held back with the sentence saying why, rather than leaving an absence to carry the answer.

items.title: Withdrawing a domain stops its mail at the next message rather than the next restart
items.body: Disabling or removing a hosted domain changes the answer port 25 gives, immediately, with no restart in between. Peers are refused permanently at the recipient, so a sender reports the failure to whoever wrote the message instead of retrying for days against a decision you meant to make. A recipient at a domain the listener started with is measured again against the hosted set as it stands at that moment rather than against the set the listener started with, which is what keeps the wire agreeing with what every management surface says about the domain. Switching a domain back on is live in the same way, provided it was hosted when the server started; a domain that was already switched off at that point needs the restart an added domain needs. That restart is the safe direction: a domain you ADD is refused until the server is restarted, which the setup sequence already requires because the acknowledgment gate is read at startup too. Publish the MX record after that restart rather than before, so the gap is not mail that bounces. A stranger refused this way is told only that this server does not handle mail for that domain, never which of the two happened or that it was once hosted here; that distinction is kept in the audit trail, where the operator can read it and the sender cannot.

items.title: A name server that goes quiet cannot hold anything open, and never passes for an answer
items.body: Inbound authentication asks the resolver questions while a peer waits: the reverse name of the connecting address, the sending domain's policy records. A resolver that accepts a question and never answers is a different failure from one that refuses, and left unbounded it would stop the session outright, holding it until the idle timeout with the peer told nothing and the connection counted against the ceiling the whole time. So those lookups carry their own deadline of forty-five seconds, and a peer that outlives it gets a temporary refusal it can retry. That is set well above anything a working resolver needs, since the resolver this server builds already bounds each of its own upstream fetches at ten seconds, so it never fires in ordinary operation. One thing it deliberately does not do is treat running out of time as an answer: a lookup that never came back is never read as a record that is not published, because that would let anyone silence a policy by stalling its query rather than by having to break it. The posture check reads the same way. `blamepost doctor` bounds every lookup it makes, so a stalled resolver cannot hold a report open with nothing on screen, and a record it could not get an answer about is reported as a third outcome rather than as a missing one. The admin view resolves nothing itself: the posture column there is the acknowledgment you recorded, and the page sends you to `blamepost doctor` for what is actually published. That distinction is the useful part: a record reported missing sends you to edit a zone that may well be correct and published, while a record reported unchecked sends you to the resolver this server reads, which is where the problem actually is. An unchecked record names neither what was expected nor what was found, because neither was observed, and a run that could not settle a record this server requires does not report itself as passing. An advisory record nobody could get an answer about is said in the summary and leaves the exit status alone, so a monitor watching the status alone should read the report rather than the number.

items.title: A body that reads as two messages is refused at the wire and again before delivery
items.body: Servers do not all agree on what ends a message, and that disagreement is how one submitted message becomes two at the receiver, the second carrying a sender nobody authenticated and inheriting the authentication of the first. Each SMTP listener refuses the shape at the point of parse, and the assembled body is measured once more at each of the two handoffs a message from the wire crosses on its way to delivery, the inbound one on port 25 and the relay one on submission. A message composed in the browser or over JMAP reaches neither handoff and cannot carry the shape in any case: the composer rewrites every bare line ending to CRLF and encodes any line that begins with a period, so there is nothing there to find. The submission listener advertises `CHUNKING`, so both spellings are reachable there and the screen runs on the chunked `BDAT` path as well as the line-by-line `DATA` one. A `BDAT` payload is an opaque byte stream under RFC 3030 §3, so it is not dot-unstuffed, and the screen applies to it anyway: the body is relayed onward and the next hop is usually `DATA`, where a bare line feed is what lets one message be read as two. A well-formed chunked message is unaffected, and a body refused when sent whole is refused when sent in chunks. A refused one is recorded under its own audit action and reaches neither a mailbox nor the spool.

items.title: An operator can see who is locked out and let them back in
items.body: A run of wrong passwords against one mailbox closes it to further attempts, which is the point, and it also means an account holder can be locked out by somebody else's guessing. A machine that mailbox has signed in from successfully within the last thirty days is let through anyway, unless that machine has spent the smaller budget kept against it, so a guessing run usually reaches the owner's newest device rather than the one they use every day. That exemption is held in the running process, so a restart drops it and the owner is then refused everywhere until the budget decays or you release it. The administration interface shows what has been locked, which budget did it, from which machine, and when it lifts on its own, and lets you release it with a recorded reason. Naming the machine matters and the page says so: the per-machine budget is read before the per-mailbox one, so releasing only the mailbox leaves the client that spent its own allowance still refused, which is the shape where an operator reports success and the account holder still cannot read mail on their phone. A machine this server cannot read as an address at all refuses the whole release rather than doing half of it, so nothing is released, the mailbox included. Refusing is the kinder answer: the table of real keys is on the same page as the form, so the cost is retyping one field, against a release that reports success while leaving untouched the very budget you were clearing. What did happen is read rather than inferred, because the notice names which budgets were released and which were left alone, and a machine you named whose budget was already clear reads differently from a machine you never named. The two mixed answers are the useful ones, and neither could be expressed while this was a single yes or no: a named machine that was already clear rules that device out and sends you to look elsewhere, while a mailbox that was already clear says the machine was the only thing refusing, which is why releasing the mailbox on its own had not helped. Each listener that authenticates also counts failures per source address on its own, and nothing releases that. The count is kept over a rolling quarter of an hour, so the refusal lifts once enough of the earliest failures have aged past that window rather than a quarter of an hour after the last one, and a source already at the ceiling records no further failures to push it out. The browser sign-in holds a bound of its own shape, counting every attempt from one address over five minutes rather than only the failures, and nothing on this page releases that one either. So a release that reports success has cleared the two budgets it names and nothing else, which is what the notice is careful to say.

items.title: Authentication failures are budgeted per identity, not only per address
items.body: An attacker rotating source addresses against one known mailbox is bounded, on the browser sign-in and on submission, IMAP, POP3 and ManageSieve alike, and the budget is shared across them so a lockout spent on one protocol is not refilled by moving to another. Passwords are hashed with Argon2id and checked against a bundled common-password list when one is set. The browser's sign-in form carries a second bound of its own, on work rather than on guessing: fifty posts in five minutes from one source address. This server reads the peer off the socket and ignores X-Forwarded-For, so with a TLS terminator in front of the browser port every reader arrives from the terminator's address and those fifty posts are one count for the whole server.

items.title: Changing a password takes effect against a sign in already under way
items.body: Signing in with a stored hash below the current Argon2id parameters replaces it, so raising the cost reaches every account as its owner signs in rather than needing a reset for each one. Argon2id is slow on purpose, which makes that replacement a long gap with the account row already read. So the stored hash is read again before the replacement is written, and the write is abandoned when it no longer matches what the sign in was working from. That is the case where it matters. Containing a credential that has been taken means changing the password, and a sign in already under way with the old one would otherwise finish by writing the old password's hash back over the new one: the change would report success, you would have confirmation you had made it, and the credential you were containing would still open the mailbox on submission, IMAP, POP3, ManageSieve and the browser. Abandoning the replacement costs nothing and never fails the sign in, because the credential it presented was correct when it presented it and the replacement is a saving on top of that answer rather than part of it.

items.title: The ARC chain is evaluated and reported, and deliberately changes nothing
items.body: A message carrying an authentication chain from an intermediary has that chain evaluated beside SPF, DKIM and DMARC, and the result is written into the Authentication-Results header your clients and filters read: none when there is no chain, pass when every seal verifies, fail when they do not. RFC 8617 gives the chain those three tokens and no more, so fail covers a seal that was checked and rejected and a sealer's key that could not be looked up alike; the mail.server.mx.envelope_verdict audit row separates the two, which is what stops a run of resolver failures reading as a run of forgeries. It moves no message. A chain is worth exactly what the party that sealed it is worth, and there is no setting here that names the intermediaries you vouch for, so a chain that validates cannot lift a DMARC failure and a broken one cannot cause a refusal. Anyone who can register a domain can seal a flawless chain over their own forgery claiming somebody else's domain passed, which is why acting on one without knowing who sealed it would be worse than not looking at all. A recipient's own Sieve script can read the result and file on it, and an account holder who subscribes to a mailing list is better placed to know they trust it than this server is.

items.title: One account cannot reach another account's folders
items.body: There is one folder namespacing scheme, and every read and every mutation an account drives resolves the acting account before it touches a folder. That layer is the only place isolation can happen: the message store underneath keeps a flat namespace of folders with no owner column, so a surface that listed folders without asking the layer that records ownership would list the whole server's. A verb that cannot identify its account refuses rather than falling back to a shared folder, on IMAP, POP3 and ManageSieve as well as in the browser and over JMAP, so no account reaches another's mail, folders or message identifiers.

items.title: Deleting an account defaults to archiving it, and erasing one reaches its mail
items.body: Destroying an account takes an explicit flag and a recorded reason, which is the deliberate act GDPR Article 17 asks for rather than the default meaning of a delete. An erasure reaches the aliases pointing at it, its mailboxes, its messages, its filter scripts, its annotations and every sealed message body no message left on this server still names, and it takes the account row last, once nothing it holds is left to name it. It runs through the same delete path IMAP EXPUNGE takes. It also reaches mail the message store still holds that no mailbox row names, which is what a delivery interrupted between its two writes leaves and which no protocol lists: those messages meet the same order and the same floor as the rest, and the audit row `blamepost.mail.mailbox.account_mail_erased` counts them apart under `messagesUnfiledErased` and `messagesUnfiledKept`, since that row is the only place an operator can account for them. So a message under a preservation order, or inside the retention floor a compliance posture sets, stays: `blamepost account remove --destroy` names each one with the mailbox it is in and the reason it stayed, keeps that mailbox so the message is still addressable, and exits non-zero only when something could not be erased for another reason. What an erasure does not reach is a backup or a snapshot taken before it ran, because a message body is sealed under the volume's key rather than under anything the erasure destroys, so set the expiry of your backups against the erasure requests you expect to answer.

items.title: An erasure destroys the mail first and the identity last, so nothing it keeps is stranded
items.body:
An erasure is partial whenever a preservation order or the retention floor keeps a message, and that is the system working: GDPR Article 17(3)(e) is the exception you answer the request with. A record you are required to produce has to stay producible, though, and every surface that could produce one resolves the account it belongs to first. So the mail goes first and the account row goes last, only once nothing still names it: no mailbox row, no filter script, no annotation and no alias. That is judged by reading the rows back rather than by what the delete path answered, and it counts everything the account holds rather than its mailboxes alone, because a filter script a governance gate held back is as unreachable as a kept message once the identity is gone.

When something is held back the account is kept and reported as kept: `blamepost account remove --destroy` opens with `Partly erased` rather than `Erased`, names each message and the rule keeping it, and says the account row was kept and why. That account is out of service from the moment the erasure runs. It refuses every credential on every listener and in the browser, and `blamepost account resume` refuses it, because the mail it held is already destroyed and nothing brings that back. It takes no delivery either: a peer naming that address at `RCPT TO` is answered `550 5.1.1` with the same sentence an address this server never held gets, before a byte of the message body is transmitted. That is permanent where the other two ways a mailbox is held are temporary, and deliberately so. A suspension and a disabled domain are lifted by the operator, so a sender should keep the message and try again; this state is not lifted, the row leaves only when the erasure finishes, and after that the address is answered `5.1.1` anyway. A temporary answer would spend the whole of the sending server's retry window against an address that can never accept the message and then return it to the person who wrote it days later, describing a condition that was never transient. It shows in `blamepost account list` as `erasing` without being asked for, so an unfinished erasure is visible rather than reading as a finished one, and running the same command again once the order is lifted or the window has passed erases what was held back and takes the row with it.

Two records say an erasure is outstanding, and the status column is only one of them. The account row carries `erasureHeldAt` beside its status, and the erasure files a chain entry of its own as it closes; the verbs that could otherwise return an account to service read both. That second record is what closes a gap the first cannot. Writing the status is one write and a volume can refuse it, because a records-retention posture puts a trigger on that column and refuses the transition itself, so the marker is attempted on its own when the transition will not land, and where neither lands the trail still answers. An account whose mark went nowhere would otherwise read as being in service with its mail already destroyed, and could be archived and then reinstated straight back into ordinary use. Whichever record is present the account reads as `erasing` and stays out of service, and archiving one is refused for the same reason reinstating it is: it would put a row whose mail is gone back within reach of reinstatement and close an erasure this server still owes.

The last two writes are answered for on the same terms as everything before them. A gate can refuse the erase of the account row itself, which leaves the account exactly where a kept filter script leaves it; the write putting the account out of service is attempted twice, once as the whole status change and once as the erasure marker on its own, and only a volume that refuses both prints `FAIL`, because then the mail is gone and the mailbox is still authenticating until you suspend it. Neither raises: by that point the mail is destroyed, and an exception in place of the report would leave nothing anywhere saying so.

Know what an order covers before you rely on it: it is placed on a message and covers the message it names, which the entry on preservation orders sets out along with what to reach for where a matter needs more than that. `blamepost blobs report` agrees with all of this: it lists mail no account holds, and mail an order or the floor is keeping does not appear there, because its account is still on the table holding it.

items.title: Signing keys leave a trail, and it names both sides of a rotation
items.body: Minting a selector, rotating one, retiring one and sweeping one out early are all recorded, and so is an attempt the signer refused: a key already active, a selector name already taken, or a selector this domain does not hold. Those are recorded because the refusal changes nothing on the volume and would otherwise leave no trace at all. An invocation turned away for a domain this server does not host, or for a name it cannot read as a domain, is answered at the terminal and not written down. An argument the signer itself refuses, a selector that is not a DNS label or a retirement naming none, is recorded like any other refusal. A rotation names the selector leaving and the selector arriving in the same row, because the question an incident asks is which key was live when a given message was signed, and that pairing exists nowhere else: the individual selector records show each half of the arriving pair being added, and each half of the outgoing pair being withdrawn when it is retired, with nothing tying the two sets together. What a row never carries is key material of either half, or any digest of it. A published key confirms a guessed private half offline without a request ever reaching this server, and nothing running here takes a value back out of the trail once it is written: only an operator archiving a range and purging it removes rows, and that is a separate act that asks before it runs. A row names a selector and an algorithm, which is what a receiver already reads off any signature this server sends.

items.title: The audit trail and the stored bodies are each checked against something outside themselves
items.body: A hash-linked chain proves that it agrees with itself, which is a weaker thing than proving nothing changed: anyone who can rewrite a row can recompute every hash that follows it. Append-only triggers stop that through this server's own database handle, and they stop nothing for somebody reaching the decrypted file outside it, where the signed checkpoints can be deleted rather than forged. So the volume keeps a separate record of where the chain stood when it was last anchored, and refuses to open when the rows disagree with that record. That record is held against the row it names in both directions: a row that hashes differently is a rewrite, and a row that is simply gone is a deletion unless a signed purge record in the database claims the range, which is the one thing that legitimately leaves a gap. That signature says who wrote the record and nothing about the rows it names, so the case is reported as a gap the run did not read rather than as one accounted for. A stored message body is checked the same way, against the digest that names its file, on every retrieval that opens the file rather than only when a reporting command happens to run. That is IMAP `FETCH` and `BODY[]`, and POP3 `RETR` and `TOP`. Webmail and JMAP render from columns inside the encrypted, authenticated database and never open the file at all, so the rename this defends against does not reach them. Sealing proves this server wrote a body. It does not prove the body is the one the row asked for, and the distance between those two statements is a single file rename.

items.title: A finding against the audit trail survives being read, and the volume stays shut until you clear it
items.body: Opening the volume anchors the chain again, which replaces the record the rows were about to be held against. So the one refusal that catches a trail rewritten in full, with its signed checkpoints deleted rather than forged, could only ever fire once: running the command a second time to be sure would have reported the volume intact. So the finding is written to audit.disputed in the data directory before the refusal is raised, and every later open reads it and refuses under the same code rather than appending to a trail nobody can stand behind. The one open that does not write it is the read-only one a reporting verb takes, which withholds the re-anchor too, so the finding is reported there and recorded by the next open that can write. Removing that file is the operator's decision and nothing does it for them. The refusals reach `blamepost audit verify-chain` as verdicts, with `--json` output a monitor can alert on, rather than as a command that crashed.

items.title: The audit trail says what it proved, and never reports a check it could not make
items.body: `blamepost audit verify-chain` reports three readings on their own lines: the chain math, the signed checkpoints, and the record beside the database. It says which of the three it made rather than reporting that nothing was inserted, altered or removed whenever the first two pass: a volume with no readable record beside it is told the rows were held against nothing outside the database they live in, which is what a volume on its first run looks like. The passing verdict is scoped to what it can actually prove: the key signing the checkpoints is sealed under the same passphrase that decrypts the database, so the guarantee is that no row was inserted, altered or removed by anyone who did not hold that passphrase. SECURITY.md, THREAT-MODEL.md and the operator guide say the same thing, and the operator guide's incident-response section explains how to tell storage damage from a rewrite and what each one calls for.

items.title: A purged range is reported as a range this server did not read
items.body:
An archive and purge deletes audit rows on purpose, and where the deletion stopped is recorded in a table inside the database. One row there discards every audit row at or below the counter it names, so the purge signs the row it writes: the signature covers the counter, the hash the row at it held and the archive the record names, under the key sealed with the vault passphrase. The volume refuses to open when that signature does not hold, and the refusal says which of the two it met, a row carrying no signature at all or a row whose signature no longer covers the range it claims, because those need opposite responses.

A signature says who wrote the record and nothing about the rows it names, so `blamepost audit verify-chain` still never reports a volume carrying one as a trail nothing was removed from. It reports `note a gap this run did not read, trusted on a signed purge boundary`, names the counter, and says plainly that no archive was verified, because nothing here verifies one: the identifier the record carries names the signed checkpoint the archive was made against rather than a location, and the archive bundle is a directory you were told to keep where this server cannot reach it. Moving a bundle off the volume is expected and changes nothing about the check. What the command can resolve is whether that checkpoint is still on the volume at or above the purged range, and it says which; a rewrite that deleted rows and relinked the survivors has to delete the checkpoints over them, so one still standing means the surviving rows were not relinked, and means nothing about the rows that are gone.

The note survives being read. Any command that opens the volume anchors the chain again over a row that is still there, so the comparison that found the gap cannot make itself twice, and a second run would otherwise report an ordinary volume. The finding is recorded in audit.disputed and repeated on every later run until you remove it. Unlike the findings recorded there for a rewritten trail, it does not shut the volume: this is a range nothing established in either direction, and refusing to deliver mail over it would be the wrong trade. To close it, read the archive bundle for the range back with `blamepost audit verify-bundle` and hold its counters against the counter in the note. If no bundle covers the range, those rows were removed rather than archived. Reading a bundle back whose covering signature could not be checked says so in the first line of the answer rather than only in the detail below it.

items.title: The audit trail is anchored while the server runs, and again when it stops
items.body:
The record beside the database is what a wholesale rewrite of the chain has to get past: a rewritten trail agrees with itself, and the signed checkpoints over it can be deleted rather than forged, so the counter and hash recorded outside the database are the witness left. That record advances only when a checkpoint is written. Opening the volume writes one, a running server writes one an hour, and a stop writes a last one: `blamepost serve` flushes the buffered rows, anchors the chain and flushes again as an ordered shutdown phase before the store closes, so a cleanly stopped volume is anchored at its newest row and the events the shutdown itself produced are on disk rather than lost with the process.

What that leaves is the hour before a server that is killed rather than stopped, and it is worth preparing for. An out of memory kill, a host reboot, a container killed rather than signaled and a power loss all end the process without a stop, and the rows written since the last hourly anchor are then covered by the chain and the checkpoints alone. Give your supervisor a stop timeout longer than the shutdown takes, so the usual case closes the window instead of bounding it. The hour is not an operator setting: no BLAMEPOST_ variable and no configuration key reaches it, and the only lever is a validated, bounded argument to `blamepost.create`, which means embedding this server rather than running the image. It is priced that way because each anchor stores a signature of about fifty kilobytes on the volume permanently and adds a few milliseconds to every later `blamepost audit verify-chain`, so a shorter interval buys a smaller window at a cost that grows for as long as the server runs. An hour in which nothing was recorded costs nothing, because there is no new tip to sign.

items.title: A refusal tells the account holder what went wrong, not where this server keeps things
items.body:
When a client asks for a message whose stored body is not on the volume, the refusal identifies it by the first sixteen characters of that body's content digest, and points at the command that reports how much of the store is affected. That is not the object id, the IMAP UID or the Message-ID, and the reply carries neither the absolute path the body would have had nor the digest in full. An ordinary account holder reaches this refusal on a plain retrieval, so anything it carried would describe the data directory's layout on disk to somebody entitled to their own mail alone. The path is nowhere in the reply, and the digest is cut to enough characters to match a message against a report and not enough to be one.

How far that match carries depends on which fault it is. `blamepost blobs report --verify` prints a body that does not match its digest under the same sixteen characters, so those line up directly. It prints a body that is missing by object id and UID with no digest at all, and missing is the fault this refusal usually reports, so hold the two together under `--json`, where the missing entry carries the digest in full. The fuller answer an operator needs is not on the wire in either case, which is why the refusal names that command. A body that does not match its digest is refused in its own terms rather than folded into the missing case, because that one means bytes changed under a file nothing rewrites.

The administration surface holds to the same line. A selector change that the signer refuses is shown to you word for word, because the signer writes those refusals for a person and they say what is already published and what to do instead. A selector change that failed for some other reason is not: a data volume that cannot be written raises a message carrying the directory the sealed private keys live in, the scheme their filenames are built from and the suffix an atomic write appends to its temporary file. That goes to the log, where a fault belongs, and the page says the change was not made and points you at it.

Which refusals count as the signer's is decided by the list of them it publishes rather than by the family its error codes belong to, because the framework underneath shares that family and writes its own faults for whoever composed it, in vocabulary naming internal functions and arguments you cannot pass. So the page shows you what the signer said about your domain and your selector, and everything else reaches the log instead.

items.title: A trail that cannot be written loses the row, not the change
items.body:
Every administrative change writes a row describing it, and that row is written after the change has already reached disk. An unreachable trail is therefore an unwritten row and nothing more: the change stands, the verb reports its own outcome rather than the trail's, and bookkeeping does not reverse work that already happened. Whether an act succeeded and whether it could be recorded are separate answers, which matters because they need opposite responses from you.

The two places that answer is worth the most are the two where the wrong reading destroys something. Generating a signing key writes the sealed private key first and the selector row second, so a refusal read as `the selector was never added` would erase the key it had just written and leave the selector published: a domain signing nothing and failing alignment on everything it sends. And restoring from a backup sets the old data directory aside, moves the bundle in, opens the result and verifies its chain before reporting success, so a refusal read as `the volume did not open` would roll the recovery back. An operator recovering from an outage is the very person whose audit sink is most likely to be unavailable, which makes that the worst available moment to lose one.

Both restore verbs say so on standard error and still exit zero, because the volume that would have held that row is the one just replaced and nothing else on the machine carries the fact. They say it in two sentences rather than one, because the two failures leave you different work: the row could not be written at all, or the row was written and could not be settled onto the volume, in which case the trail may carry it after all. Rows are written before the verb returns rather than buffered, so this costs no durability, and a deletion that has to be provable is unaffected: a deletion is additionally recorded by the framework's own erasure path.

items.title: The administration surface records what it refused and what it canceled
items.body:
Two things a console does are only worth anything if you can read them back afterwards, and both are on the trail.

An account that does not administer this server is turned away from every administration page and every administration form, and that refusal is recorded, naming the account and the exact verb it asked for. A signed-in mailbox owner working through the console by hand is the event an incident is reconstructed from, and it is the stronger signal of the two: a caller with no session at all leaves a row of the framework's own, while this one names somebody who is already inside.

Canceling a queued message erases it from the volume, so the trail is where the answer lives. The queue page asks why, records a row per canceled message naming you, the message, the recipient it was for, your reason and whether the sender was written to, and files it under the same name the `blamepost queue` command uses, so one filter finds both. It also does not act on a message it no longer holds. Selecting a message that has since gone out, ended in a report, or been canceled from another window says so rather than reporting a cancellation, because telling an operator working through a compromised account's outbound mail that a message is gone when it is not is the one answer this page must never give.

items.title: A signing key that will not open names its domain and its selector, and signs nothing
items.body:
Every DKIM private key is sealed on the data volume, and three things leave one unusable: the file is not there, it is there and carries no seal, or it is there and does not open. Signing runs on every message an account submits, so each of those is answered where an operator can act on it. The refusal names the domain, the selector and the algorithm, says which of the three it met, and prints the way out with the pair's selector already filled in: restore the volume from a backup taken before it happened, or retire the pair and mint a replacement. A key that opens for nobody here was either written under a different volume's vault key or damaged where it lies, and those two are indistinguishable from the outside, so the refusal names both rather than choosing one. A passphrase that does not fit is neither and never reaches this point, because it stops the server at start.

A file carrying no seal is refused rather than signed with. This server seals every private key it writes, so a key file that is not sealed was put there by something else and has been readable to anyone who could read the volume for as long as it has been there. That refusal says to treat the pair as exposed and to withdraw its records immediately rather than after the usual overlap.

None of the three carries the data directory, the key filename scheme or any part of the volume's layout, because a refusal the signer writes is one an administration page is allowed to show word for word; these three reach the log and the audit trail, since signing happens on the send path rather than on a page. Mail from the domain still relays unsigned meanwhile, since a key problem is not a reason to refuse an account's own mail. The reason it went unsigned is recorded under a code you can filter on, and is told apart from a domain that simply has no keys yet.

items.title: Mail sent from the browser or over JMAP leaves the same trail as mail sent over submission
items.body:
A message that could not be signed still goes out, because a key problem is not a reason to refuse an account's own mail, so the audit row is the only place that fact ever surfaces. That makes the row's outcome load-bearing: it is what you filter on while working out why a domain's DMARC reports have started arriving, and a send filed as a success would answer with the opposite of what happened.

So every surface that composes a message files the same thing: a failure, naming the domain, carrying the signer's code in a field of its own, and split across two names so a domain still waiting for its first key pair is not filed as one whose key has gone. `blamepost audit read --action blamepost.mail.compose.unsigned_no_key` finds the first and `--action blamepost.mail.compose.unsigned` the second, beside the two names the submission listener already writes, and mail submitted over JMAP files under that same pair, since it is composed here rather than on the submission port. An alert wants all four names. A line naming the domain also goes to the log as the message leaves, so a fault you are already watching for does not wait to be asked about.

items.title: Every RSA DKIM selector this server mints is 2048 bits
items.body: 2048 is the current DKIM key-strength guidance and the 2024 bulk-sender floor, and it is what every RSA selector minted here gets. There is no setting that lowers it: the size is not an environment variable or a configuration key, and the signer refuses to be built at all below the floor rather than carrying a smaller number down to the key generator and relaying whatever the generator says about its own options. The framework underneath still admits 1024 as an opt-in; nothing here takes it.

items.title: A sealed key that will not open has two causes, and the passphrase is not one of them
items.body:
A sealed TLS private key that will not open cannot mean the passphrase has changed, and the certificate report does not send you to check it. The passphrase opens the vault while the server is starting, and one that does not fit stops the boot right there, so any read that runs at all is running under a passphrase that fitted. Checking it would cost an afternoon on the one thing already proven correct.

So the report names the two causes that are left. The file was written under a different volume's vault key, or its bytes have been damaged where they lie. Restore it from a backup taken from before the damage, or write the unsealed pair to the two paths this server reads.

The browser surface takes the same key through the same seal on its way to binding the TLS port, and refuses in those same words, so the sentence you read does not depend on which of the two showed it to you.

items.title: The console names what it is about to destroy and asks you to type it back
items.body:
Five acts on the administration pages cannot be taken back from those pages: archiving an account, withdrawing a hosted domain, removing an alias, retiring a signing pair, and canceling messages off the outbound queue. Each of them is one button on a list of rows that all look alike, and a row is chosen with a mouse.

So each of them takes two posts. The first changes nothing and answers with a page naming exactly what is about to happen and what it reaches. The second has to carry a value read off that page and typed back: the account's address, the domain name, the alias address (or the domain, where the alias is a catch-all), the selector, or how many of the messages you picked are still waiting. A page cannot supply that on your behalf, which is the whole difference between a confirmation and a hidden field, and none of it is a dialog the browser puts up: a browser can be told to stop showing those and nothing about one reaches the server, so this is checked here, against state read here.

The count is the one that does more than slow you down. It is measured again at the moment of the act, so a message that reaches its recipient, ends in a report, or is canceled from another window between the two posts no longer matches, and nothing is erased under a page that has gone stale.

The reversible acts do not ask you to type anything back, deliberately, because a console that asked for a typed value on everything teaches an operator to type through the question, which is the same as not asking. Suspending an account, putting a domain back in service, and giving or taking back the operator role each ask for the reason they record and nothing more. Reinstating an account, adding a domain or an alias, minting and rotating a pair, withdrawing selectors whose overlap has already run out, and forcing the queue change on one press. An archived account carries the button that reinstates it, so the list offers the way back rather than leaving one off by omission.

items.title: The reason an administrative row records is the one the operator typed
items.body:
Suspending an account, archiving one, withdrawing a domain, removing an alias and canceling a queued message each write an audit row with a reason column of its own, and that column is what somebody reading the trail afterwards has to go on. Each of them asks the operator for it and refuses without one in the layer that performs the act rather than in the browser, so that layer is the authority on whether it may proceed. Canceling a queued message carries a second demand of the same kind: the spool's own remove verb also refuses a caller that has not said whether the sender of the canceled message is written to, so no surface can settle that by leaving it out.

A form that filled the column in on the operator's behalf would be worse than one that left it empty. A reason that is present and identical on every row reads like somebody wrote it, so a trail full of them answers nothing while looking as though it does, and an absent one is at least visibly absent. Where a verb genuinely warrants no typed reason, the layer performing it records its own account of the run instead: retiring a signing pair records the selectors it retired and the keys it erased, and the signer's own sentence where it refused, rather than a sentence collected by a form and thrown away.

items.title: Canceling queued mail never writes to an address a stranger chose
items.body:
Canceling a message off the outbound queue erases it, so its sender would otherwise be left believing it went out. Which sender gets told depends on which of the two kinds of message it is, and the console tells them apart before it writes to anybody.

A message relayed after an authenticated submission carries a reverse path bound to the account that authenticated, because the submission listener refuses a MAIL FROM the account does not own. That address is a mailbox here and its owner is exactly who needs telling. A message an alias is forwarding off this server is the other kind: its reverse path arrived on the inbound wire, whoever sent the message chose it, and nothing has ever checked it against anything. Reporting to that turns one press of a button into mail from this server to an address somebody else picked, which is backscatter, and the incident runbook sends an operator to this page during exactly the event that fills a queue with it.

The rule is that a report this page generates is only ever addressed to a domain this server hosts, so it is delivered here or refused here and never reaches an address somebody else picked. A reverse path in a hosted domain is written to; anything else is not written to at all, the empty reverse path included, for the reason RFC 5321 section 6.1 gives. The page says which of your selection falls on each side before you confirm, and the row for each canceled message records whether the sender was told, so an operator who does need to reach a legitimate remote sender has the recipient and the reverse path in front of them instead of an assumption that everybody was told.

items.title: The console will not take itself away from every administrator
items.body:
Four forms on the administration pages could leave this server with nobody able to sign in to it: suspending the last administrator, archiving them, taking the operator role from them, and withdrawing the domain that administrator's address belongs to, since an account is only usable while its domain is. Any of the four and the console is shut to everyone, with no way back through the browser, because the administrator role is granted from these pages and there are no pages left to grant it from.

What that costs is more than the mistake looks like. The command line verbs that put an account or a domain back need the data volume, and the running server holds it, so recovering means stopping the server: every listener down and mail queued at the sending side until somebody notices. Each of the four measures who would still be able to sign in afterwards and refuses when the answer is nobody, naming the way forward: give another account the role first, or, for the three that have a host verb, stop the server and run it from there. Taking the role names none, because the console is the only place the role is granted, and naming a verb that does not exist would send you to a terminal to find out. The refusal is recorded whichever way you arrived at it, because somebody reaching for the one action that closes the console is worth reading about afterwards.

It refuses on that reading alone and never on the verb. Suspending an administrator, archiving one, or taking the role back while another administrator remains all go through, and so does withdrawing a domain that holds no administrator, which is what keeps containment available: an account whose password has been taken is closed from the console in the ordinary way as long as you are not the last one left, and from the host with the server stopped when you are. The identity layer carries no check of its own, so `blamepost account suspend` and `blamepost domain disable` refuse nothing here.
